records.title: ENH Add argument to `SelectFwe` to choose between Bonferroni and Holm method
records.body: ### Describe the workflow you want to enable ### Problem Feature selection is frequently used to reduce the dimensionality of large datasets. To this end, a univariate scoring function can be used to test the hypothesis that a feature correlates with a variable of interest. However, testing a large group of features introduces the multiple comparisons problem where the type I error probability (i.e., the probability of erroneously rejecting a null hypothesis that the feature _does not_ correlate) exceeds the nominal error probability for the whole test family due to the large number of tests performed. A feature may thus appear to correlate with the target variable merely due to noise and end up getting selected erroneously. `sklearn.feature_selection.SelectFwe` implements the Bonferroni correction which ensures that the actual type I error probability corresponds to the nominal error probability by dividing the significance threshold for each individual p value per feature by the total number of tests. This textbook procedure, however, comes with the risk of increasing the type II error probability, i.e., the error of failing to reject the null hypothesis when it is in fact false. This may result in a failure to detect features although they are informative in reality. The [Holm method](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Holm%E2%80%93Bonferroni_method) (a.k.a. Holm-Bonferroni method) solves this problem by providing the same protection against type I errors as Bonferroni while reducing the probability of a type II error. In other words, it controls the family-wise error rate as effectively as the Bonferroni correction but is more sensitive to informative features, thereby reducing the risk of missing a feature that in fact does correlate with a target variable. Although the Holm method is more powerful than Bonferroni, it unfortunately is not currently implemented in SelectFwe. ### Availability in other software packages The Holm method is commonplace in other (statistics) software like [R](https://www.rdocumentation.org/packages/stats/versions/3.6.2/topics/p.adjust) or Python's [`statsmodels` library](https://www.statsmodels.org/dev/generated/statsmodels.stats.multitest.multipletests.html) where it is the default method to control the family-wise error rate. ### Describe your proposed solution I modified `SelectFwe` so that it now accepts an additional input argument called `fwe_control` of type `str`. The user can choose between "bonf" for Bonferroni, which is its default setting for better backward compatibility, and "holm" for the Holm method. The Holm method sorts all m null hypotheses of a test family by their corresponding p values in ascending order $p_1 The example shows that the Holm method controls the family-wise error rate while detecting more informative features compared to the Bonferroni correction. The difference between the two measures is expected to scale with the number of input features. ### Describe alternatives you've considered, if relevant _No response_ ### Additional context I first submitted this feature request as a PR, which is available [here](https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/pull/33409). The reviewer suggested that I first open an issue to provide the community with the opportunity to discuss the idea first.

records.title: RFC Improving guidance for common CI failures for new contributors
records.body: > [!WARNING] This issue is currently under discussion and not open for contributions at this time. Disclosure: I used ChatGPT to proofread earlier drafts of this issue. All mistakes are due to me. TL;DR: This RFC is to discuss how to help beginners ensure their PRs have all CI checks passing, so they are easier to review. Some beginners may not realise that CI is running against their PRs, or may find it difficult to interpret and act on the error messages from failing checks. This was my situation in my first PR to the project https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/pull/27913. I needed to be told explicitly that I should address CI failures and how to approach them https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/pull/27913#issuecomment-1973884884. As a result, some PRs end up sitting with failing CI without further updates. At the same time, reviewers often need to repeat similar guidance across many PRs, and given the limited reviewer bandwidth, these PRs may not always receive timely feedback. This can slow down the onboarding process for new contributors. From what I've seen, a few types of CI failures come up repeatedly for beginners: * Linting issues * Failing unit tests * Code coverage drops Perhaps we could group guidance for these common cases in one place, and complement it with automated messages, so contributors can more easily resolve issues on their own without waiting for reviewer feedback. More precisely, I propose the following: 1. Add a short paragraph in the [Contributing Guide](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/developers/contributing.html) (e.g., in the [pull request checklist](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/developers/contributing.html#pull-request-checklist)) noting that having all CI checks passing helps make a PR easier to review and prioritise. * #34239 1. Add a “Common CI Failures and How to Resolve Them” section in the [Contributing Guide](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/developers/contributing.html), documenting recurring issues (e.g. linting, tests, coverage) along with concrete steps to fix them (such as using `pre-commit`, running `pytest` locally, etc.). 1. Extend `github actions bot` comments to point to the relevant sections of this guide when certain checks fail. For example, similar to how `pre-commit` is suggested when linting fails, we could provide targeted pointers for test failures and coverage drops. I'm not very familiar with the current CI setup or GitHub Actions configuration, so I'm not sure how feasible all of this is, but I hope this can serve as a starting point for discussion on making these PRs easier to move forward. Cc'ing @lesteve and @GaelVaroquaux for visibility. --- Edit: Added Warning

records.body: ### Describe the bug and give evidence about its user-facing impact For instance, if you have a small value (such as 1e-6, 1e-12), it is displayed as 0. In some cases it can be misleading because you know that this value is expected to be non-zero as in the following cases: ### Steps/Code to Reproduce ```python from sklearn.linear_model import RidgeCV import numpy as np rng = np.random.RandomState(0) y = rng.randn(100) X = y[:, None] alphas = np.logspace(-12, 12, 13) regressor = RidgeCV(alphas=alphas).fit(X, y) regressor ``` The displayed value for `alpha_` is surprising because we know that it's supposed to belong to one of the `alphas` passed as argument: ```python >>> alphas array([1.e-12, 1.e-10, 1.e-08, 1.e-06, 1.e-04, 1.e-02, 1.e+00, 1.e+02, 1.e+04, 1.e+06, 1.e+08, 1.e+10, 1.e+12]) ``` And if you look at the fitted attribute interactively, it's rendered "correctly" by jupyter/IPython: ```python >>> regressor.alpha_ 1e-12 ``` ### Expected Results The HTML display should use an alternative string representation for float attributes with a less misleading way of rounding, for instance '1e-12' as rendered by the following formatting string that should use 4 numerical digits using the scientific notation: ```python >>> f"{regressor.alpha_:.4g}" '1e-12' ``` or: ```python >>> f"{regressor.alpha_:.4e}" '1.0000e-12' ``` ### Actual Results See the rendered HTML table above. ### Versions ```shell Today's `main` branch (1.9.dev0). ``` ### Interest in fixing the bug I don't want to fix the bug myself if @DeaMariaLeon is interested in working on a PR for this.

records.body:
### Describe the bug and give evidence about its user-facing impact

ColumnTransformer.fit raises KeyError('remainder') when metadata routing is enabled, and a child transformer requests sample_weight, and remainder='passthrough'. I want to be able to specify remainder as passthrough, and and also use metadata routing, specifically for transformers that need a sample_weight to be provided. This works on scikit-learn 1.7.2.

### Steps/Code to Reproduce

```python
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import sklearn
from sklearn import set_config
from sklearn.base import BaseEstimator, TransformerMixin
from sklearn.compose import ColumnTransformer

print(f"scikit-learn version: {sklearn.__version__}")

set_config(enable_metadata_routing=True)
print(
    "enable_metadata_routing:",
    sklearn.get_config()["enable_metadata_routing"],
)

X = pd.DataFrame(
    {
        "x1": [1.0, 2.0, 3.0],
        "x2": [22.0, 38.0, 26.0],
        "x3": [7.25, 71.2833, 7.925],
    }
)
y = pd.Series([0, 1, 1], name="survived")
sample_weight = pd.Series(np.ones(len(X)), name="sample_weight")

class MyTransformer(TransformerMixin, BaseEstimator):
    def fit(self, X, y=None, sample_weight=None):
        print("fit called, with sample_weight:", sample_weight)
        return self

    def transform(self, X):
        print("transform called")

mt = MyTransformer().set_fit_request(sample_weight=True)

records.title: Redundant sparse checks in linear_model/_base.py causing unnecessary repeated issparse() calls
records.body:
### Describe the bug and give evidence about its user-facing impact

There is a small redundancy in `sklearn/linear_model/_base.py` where `sp.issparse()` is called multiple times on the same variables (`X` and `y`).

The condition first checks:
if sp.issparse(X) or sp.issparse(y):

Then later, the same checks are repeated separately:
if sp.issparse(X):
...
if sp.issparse(y):

This leads to unnecessary repeated function calls, which can be avoided by caching the results in boolean variables.

Impact: Minor performance inefficiency and reduced code clarity. While it does not break functionality, it introduces avoidable redundancy in a frequently used code path.

### Steps/Code to Reproduce

```python
import numpy as np
import scipy.sparse as sp
from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression

# Create sparse data
X = sp.csr_matrix(np.random.rand(100, 10))
y = sp.csr_matrix(np.random.rand(100, 1))

model = LinearRegression()
model.fit(X, y)

# No error occurs, but internally issparse() is called multiple times redundantly
```

### Expected Results

Sparse checks should be performed once and reused via cached boolean variables to avoid redundant calls.

### Actual Results

The code runs correctly, but `sp.issparse()` is called multiple times on the same variables, leading to minor inefficiency and less optimal code structure.

### Versions

```shell
import sklearn
sklearn.show_versions()
```

### Interest in fixing the bug

Yes, I would be interested in working on a PR.

Root cause: Repeated calls to `sp.issparse()` instead of caching results.

Proposed fix:
Cache results using:
X_is_sparse = sp.issparse(X)
y_is_sparse = sp.issparse(y)

Then reuse these variables in all subsequent conditions.

This improves readability and avoids redundant computation.

records.title: Duplicate check_array parameter usage in pairwise.py for X and Y inputs
records.body:
### Describe the bug and give evidence about its user-facing impact

In `sklearn/metrics/pairwise.py` (lines ~167–202), `check_array` is called with identical parameters for both `X` and `Y` when they are different objects.

Current behavior:
- If `Y is X` or `Y is None`, `check_array` is called once.
- Otherwise, `check_array` is called separately for both `X` and `Y` using the same arguments.

This leads to duplicated parameter passing and slightly reduced code maintainability. Additionally, `_find_floating_dtype_allow_sparse` already processes both inputs, making this repetition unnecessary from a structural perspective.

Impact: No functional issue, but introduces redundancy and reduces code clarity.

### Steps/Code to Reproduce

```python
import numpy as np
from sklearn.metrics.pairwise import cosine_similarity

X = np.random.rand(100, 10)
Y = np.random.rand(100, 10)

cosine_similarity(X, Y)

# Internally, check_array is called twice with identical parameters
```

### Expected Results

Common parameters for `check_array` should be consolidated to avoid duplication and improve readability.

### Actual Results

`check_array` is invoked separately for `X` and `Y` with identical parameters, leading to duplicated code paths.

### Versions

```shell
import sklearn
sklearn.show_versions()
```

### Interest in fixing the bug

No, I would be interested in working on a PR.

My approach:
- Extract common `check_array` parameters into a shared configuration.
- Apply the same configuration to both `X` and `Y` without duplicating argument definitions.
- Ensure behavior remains unchanged by running existing tests.

Additionally, I would review nearby code for similar duplication patterns and refactor them where applicable to improve overall consistency.

records.title: Unnecessary y.ndim check and separate array transformations in _forest.py
records.body:
### Describe the bug and give evidence about its user-facing impact

In `sklearn/ensemble/_forest.py` (lines ~375–378), `y` is checked for `ndim == 1` and then reshaped. Later, a separate check ensures dtype and contiguity using `np.ascontiguousarray`.

Current behavior:
- `y` is reshaped when 1D.
- Later, dtype and contiguity are handled separately.

This leads to fragmented array transformations, where reshape and dtype/contiguity handling are done in multiple steps.

Impact: No functional issue, but introduces redundancy and reduces code clarity. The later `np.ascontiguousarray` call could handle dtype conversion and memory layout in a more consolidated way.

### Steps/Code to Reproduce

```python
import numpy as np
from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestClassifier

X = np.random.rand(100, 5)
y = np.random.randint(0, 2, size=100)  # 1D target

model = RandomForestClassifier()
model.fit(X, y)

# Internally, y is reshaped and later processed again for dtype/contiguity
```

### Expected Results

Array transformations (reshape, dtype conversion, contiguity) should be consolidated into a single, clear step where possible.

### Actual Results

Reshape and dtype/contiguity handling are performed in separate steps, leading to slightly redundant processing and reduced readability.

### Versions

```shell
import sklearn
sklearn.show_versions()
```

### Interest in fixing the bug

I am not planning to submit a PR for this issue. Sharing it so that maintainers or contributors can address it if deemed useful.

records.title: ENH: Add FARC-HD (Fuzzy Association Rule-based Classification Model for High-Dimensional problems)
records.body:
### Describe the workflow you want to enable

Currently, scikit-learn lacks native support for robust Fuzzy Logic-based classifiers, specifically those optimized for high-dimensional datasets. Researchers and practitioners often have to rely on external, outdated tools to run these types of algorithms, which breaks the standard Python data science workflow. I would like to propose the inclusion of the FARC-HD classifier to allow users to build fuzzy rule-based pipelines natively.

### Describe your proposed solution

I have developed a fully functional Python implementation of the FARC-HD algorithm (Alcalá-Fdez et al., 2011). My current implementation closely follows the scikit-learn API, inheriting from BaseEstimator and ClassifierMixin, and processes standard NumPy arrays seamlessly.

**Inclusion Criteria Check:**
The algorithm meets the strict inclusion criteria for scikit-learn:

- Age: The original paper was published in 2011.

- Citations: The core paper "A Fuzzy Association Rule-Based Classification Model for High-Dimensional Problems with Genetic Rule Selection and Lateral Tuning" has over 470 citations on Google Scholar, far exceeding the 200+ threshold.

- Relevance: It is a highly cited and well-established baseline for fuzzy classification in complex spaces.

**Technical Architecture & Dependency Considerations:**
Currently, my working prototype uses numba for JIT compilation to handle the heavy mathematical computations of the fuzzy logic rules efficiently.

I am aware of scikit-learn's general preference to avoid heavy dependencies like Numba in the core library. If the core developers agree that FARC-HD is a valuable addition, I would be open to exploring the possibility of porting the performance-critical sections to Cython, should you deem it strictly necessary for integration.

### Describe alternatives you've considered, if relevant

The main alternative is publishing this as an independent PyPI package or submitting it to scikit-learn-contrib (where Numba is generally accepted). While I am evaluating those routes, I believe FARC-HD's academic standing makes it a strong candidate for native inclusion in the core library.

### Additional context

Would you be open to discussing the potential inclusion of this algorithm and the acceptable technical approach to handle the computational bottlenecks?

records.title: [Callbacks] Should/Can we avoid creating the context tree when no callbacks ?
records.body:
For meta-estimators, the answer is a definitive no. They can have subestimators with callbacks which need the full context tree to work optimally.

For regular estimators, it could make sense. The performance for creating contexts is not prohibitive: ~1-2us. This is small for one iteration even for quick estimators and small datasets (knowing that callbacks don't go deeper than iterations involving the full dataset). But there might be cases where it matters.

I would avoid doing it if it adds too much verbosity within every estimator, like adding conditional branches everywhere we create a subcontext or call callback hooks. But if we can enable the feature without changing the existing callback support api implementation, why not.

records.title: Add 'auto' option to `n_bins` in `calibration_curve`
records.body:
### Problem

Currently, the `n_bins` parameter in [`sklearn.calibration.calibration_curve`](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/generated/sklearn.calibration.calibration_curve.html) defaults to 5. This is often suboptimal for datasets of varying sizes, especially for large datasets. Users must manually tune this parameter to balance the trade-off between bias (too few bins) and variance (too many bins).

Example: for a dataset of size $n = 100,000$, the optimal number of bins is on the order of 100, far exceeding the default 5. Using the default 5 creates a calibration curve that's overly crude.

### Describe your proposed solution
Specifically, research in the paper ["Optimal Recalibration via Uniform-Mass Binning"](https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.5555/3666122.3669166) provides a theoretical proof that the optimal number of bins ($B$) for recalibration via uniform-mass binning scales with the cubic root of the number of samples ($n$). (Conflict of interest: I'm an author of the paper)

The proposed implementation would be:
```python
if n_bins == 'auto':
    n_bins = int(len(y_true) ** (1/3))
```

Benefits include:
* **Ease of Use**: Tuning free. This is also the practice for many other sklearn implementation of algorithms, e.g.,
  * `max_features` of `RandomForestClassifier` defaults to `sqrt`, which uses $\sqrt{n\\_features}$ for classifiers.
  * `gamma` of `SVC` has options `'scale'` and `'auto'`.
* **Statistical Robustness**: defaulting to a theoretically optimal value improves the reliability of calibration metrics and plots across a wider range of $n$.

### Describe alternatives you've considered, if relevant

Maybe `'cubic-root'` or `'optimal'` will be more descriptive than `'auto'`?

### Additional context

Here's a rough description of why $\sqrt{n}$ is the optimal bin number (under some quite general assumptions):
- **Notations**: Let $Z$ be the random variable of the predicted probability to be calibrated, and $h^\star$ be the optimal calibration function $h^\star(z) := \text{E}[Y|Z=z]$.
- **Bound of bias**: First, each bins has about $n/B$ samples, which contributes to $B/n$ factor in the calibration risk bound due to Hoeffding's inequality.
- **Bound of variance**: Then, we note the sharpness risk $\text{E}[\text{Var}(h^\star(Z)) | h(Z))]$ is the average conditional variance of $h^\star(Z)$ in each bin. Since the variance is smaller than the squared range, and the range of $h^\star(Z)$ within each bin is bounded by $O(1/B)$, we have the average conditional variance is bounded by O(1/B^2).
- **Bound of MSE**: Lastly, minimizing the sum of the two bounds $O(1/B^2 + B/n)$ yields $B \asymp n^{1/3}$.

records.title: Docs are not explicit about effect of set_params
records.body:
### Describe the issue linked to the documentation

There is quite a bit of documentation for developing scikit-learn-compatible estimators:
https://scikit-learn.org/stable/developers/develop.html

They mention for example that `__init__` should not validate parameters:
https://scikit-learn.org/stable/developers/develop.html#instantiation

And they mention that calling `.fit()` should set attributes with underscores as needed:
https://scikit-learn.org/stable/developers/develop.html#estimated-attributes

But they aren't explicit about one important detail: is the object state after fitting meant to be alterable by `.set_params()`? And if so, should that trigger re-calculations of fitted attributes for example?

For example, should the following sequences be equivalent in order for an estimator to be compatible with scikit-learn?
* `estimator.fit(...).set_output(...).predict(...)`
* `estimator.fit(...).predict(...)`

As far as I can see, most scikit-learn estimators that have some behavior that depends on input parameters after fitting make a copy of the attribute that they used with an underscore - e.g. KNN classes save an 'effective metric', PCA saves `n_components_`, and so on.

But there are cases where it doesn't work like that - e.g.:
```python
import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(seed=123)
X = rng.standard_normal(size=(1000,10))

from sklearn.neighbors import LocalOutlierFactor

LocalOutlierFactor().fit(X).set_params(novelty=True).predict(X)
# vs.
LocalOutlierFactor().fit(X).predict(X)
```

### Suggest a potential alternative/fix

Would be quite helpful if the doc could be more explicit about how `set_params` should or shouldn't affect the estimator state after a first call to `.fit()` has been made.

Imagine for example a case where calls to `.predict()` use different attributes according to some input parameter that's settable through `.set_params()`.

records.title: Hopefully Helpful (AI) Contributing Policy Proposal
records.body:
I saw a [video](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ssTUhnShKGM) about the Open Source Community problems related to AI Contributing and I saw your [Issue](https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/issues/31679) related to that.

In another video, there was also mention of a proposed solution that GitHub could even have developed.
2 months later, GitHub has still not developed it, and there was a video in recent days suggesting that it might actually be better that GitHub did not develop it.
https://github.com/marketplace/actions/ai-pull-request-equalizer#credits

So I made a very simple GitHub Action:

- If someone has a defined — configurable — permission on GitHub (for example admin/pull), then they can open a PR.
- If someone has at least 1 open Issue assigned to them, they can open a PR.
- If they do not meet either of the above conditions, then they receive a message to channel their energy to a place where there is a shortage of them.

This is a bit different from your current 'You can open PRs to not Needs Triage Issues after commenting under them'.

If you find it useful, then in your current flow I could imagine it as follows:
- Either you allow an always open issue for an external contributor (for example a 'I am not an AI introduction: I would like to contribute to scikit-learn' issue)
- Or you explicitly assign the issue to the person who indicated in a comment that they are working on it. (A human contributor takes far more time than this to complete it, and the AI contributor does not have a sense of time, it does not wait)

Why I think my solution is better than the competing ones:
Simple installation (you only need to copy+paste one file), transparent rules and It redirects AI contributors instead of blocking them — less likely to trigger a strong reaction.

If I have piqued your interest, you can find it here:
https://github.com/marketplace/actions/ai-pull-request-equalizer

records.body:
I noticed that numpy recently updated their PR template (https://github.com/numpy/numpy/pull/30932) which now includes a section where the contributor should introduce himself (if first time contributor). I found that quite interesting for our struggle with the flood of fully automated PRs.

They added the following instruction
```
### First time committer introduction
<!-- If you are new to the NumPy community, please introduce yourself. How do you
 use NumPy, what prompted you to make this contribution? We are a community of
 mostly volunteers, and getting to know you helps us trust your judgement
 and welcome you into the community.
-->
```

What do you think ?

records.title: [Callbacks] VS Code debugger fails with `EOFError` during Callback instance creation
records.body:
Creating a callback instance works in a normal test run, but fails when run in the VS Code debugger. This started after #33649.

This may not only be a hurdle for my own developing workflow, but also for third party devs in the future.

Reproducible:

```py
def test_debugger_process():
    TestingCallback()
    print('Fine!')
```

runs fine, but fails with `EOFError` when used with VS Code debugger on Linux and with Python 3.14.2.

records.title: Add replaced_undefined_by in classification metrics
records.body:
Following https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/issues/29048 and in particular https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/issues/29048#issuecomment-2857931743, we want to replace ``zero_division`` by a ``replaced_undefined_by`` parameter to the following classification metrics:

- [ ] ``jaccard_score``
- [ ] ``f1_score``
- [ ] ``fbeta_score``
- [ ] ``precision_recall_fscore_support``
- [ ] ``precision_score``
- [ ] ``recall_score``
- [ ] ``classification_report``

In these metrics, ``zero_division`` should be deprecated and ``replaced_undefined_by`` with the following behavior:
- default to ``nan``
- when the metric is undefined: raise an UndefinedMetricWarning and return ``replaced_undefined_by``
- the warning message should explain the reason for the metric to be undefined

We also want to add a ``replaced_undefined_by`` parameter the following classification metrics:
- [ ] ``balanced_accuracy_score``
- [ ] ``matthews_corrcoef``

We may also want to add the param to some metrics in ``_ranking.py``:
- [ ] ``ndcg_score``

(The lists will be updated when we identify metrics that need it)

records.title: Use clang-cl (LLVM) compiler for Windows ARM64 wheel builds
records.body:
### Describe the workflow you want to enable

Scikit-learn currently ships ARM64 Windows wheels built with MSVC. This proposal is to switch the Windows ARM64 wheel build to use **clang-cl** in the CI pipeline for improved performance and build reliability.

 **Initial scikit-learn implementation already exists**
  A working PR switching the win_arm64 CI wheel build to clang-cl was raised and demonstrates the change builds and passes tests successfully.
   [scikit-learn PR #33435](https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/pull/33435)

**Motivation:**

The need for clang-cl on Windows ARM64 is well documented across the ecosystem:

 **CPython acknowledged the ARM64 Windows performance gap**
  Python release binaries on ARM64 Windows show significantly lower performance compared to x64, traced to MSVC's weaker ARM64  auto-vectorisation. This is the upstream root cause that affects all Python packages built with MSVC on this platform.
  [python/cpython #134524](https://github.com/python/cpython/issues/134524)

 **Community discussion on clang-cl for Windows ARM64**
  A dedicated thread on Python.org Ideas discusses using clang-cl to address the performance gap in Windows ARM64 Python packages, with broad agreement from the scientific Python community that LLVM is the right path forward for this platform.
   [Python.org Discussions](https://discuss.python.org/t/using-clang-cl-for-better-performance-on-windows-on-arm/)

  **NumPy formally proposed and adopted clang-cl for win_arm64**
  NumPy raised this as an enhancement issue to provide Windows ARM64 wheels compiled with the LLVM toolchain, citing the same MSVC  ARM64 vectorisation gap. This was subsequently implemented and NumPy now ships win_arm64 wheels built with clang-cl.
    [numpy/numpy #29174](https://github.com/numpy/numpy/issues/29174)
    [numpy/numpy #28106](https://github.com/numpy/numpy/issues/28106)
    [numpy/numpy PR #28246](https://github.com/numpy/numpy/pull/28246)

NumPy and SciPy
scikit-learn's two core dependencies already ship win_arm64 wheelsbuilt with clang-cl.


### Describe your proposed solution

Switch the `win_arm64` CI wheel build from MSVC to **clang-cl** (LLVM). The change is scoped to Windows ARM64 only all other platforms (win_amd64, Linux, macOS) remain unchanged.

**Test suite**

All scikit-learn tests pass with the clang-cl build. The implementation includes a fix for a `uint32_t` redefinition that
occurs specifically with clang-cl on Windows.

### Describe alternatives you've considered, if relevant

_No response_

### Additional context

_No response_

records.title: Add `MoveTo` transformer to move `X` to a different array namespace/device
records.body:
> [!WARNING]
> This issue is not yet ready for a PR. If you are interested in contributing to scikit-learn, please have a look at our [contributing guidelines](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html), and in particular the sections for [new contributors](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#new-contributors) and the ["Needs triage"](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#issues-tagged-needs-triage) label.

This issue describes a new transformer `MoveTo` that can be used to move `X` to another array namespace and device. The goal of the transformer is to move the input array `X` to a specified array namespace (numpy, torch, cupy) and device (CPU, CUDA, MPS, etc). The transformer can not move `y` or `sample_weight` but that is Ok, because of https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/issues/28668.

The goal is to [enable a `Pipeline` like the following](https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/issues/31274#issuecomment-2884368423) when using the experimental support for array API (and other use-cases where processing has to move from one namespace/device to another):

```python
df = pd.read_parquet("data_file.parquet")
X = df[categorical_feature_names]  # categorical or str/object dtype
y = df[target_column_name]  # continuous value to regress.

pipeline = make_pipeline(
   TargetEncoder(),  # works on categorical X but also needs y, hence CPU for both
   MoveTo(namespace=torch, device="cuda:0"),
   Ridge(),  # only numerical inputs: faster to do it all on GPU, y follows X => y_pred on GPU.
)

cv_results = cross_validate(pipeline, X, y, scoring="r2")
```

Currently you can make the example above work by replacing `MoveTo` with `FunctionTransformer(partial(torch.asarray, device="cuda:0"))`. However it is difficult for the average user to discover this particular `FunctionTransformer` incantation and looking towards the future where we want to offer a function that can "translate" a whole pipeline from running on one namespace/device to another (e.g. train on GPU, then deploy on CPU) having an explicitly named step that can be specially treated is useful.


xref https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/issues/33444

records.title: DOC: Improve warnings and recommendations for LeaveOneOut and LeavePOut
records.body:
### Current Problem

In `LeaveOneOut` and `LeavePOut` classes (`sklearn/model_selection/_split.py`), the documentation mentions that these methods "can be very costly" for large datasets, but the warning is quite vague.

Users often try these on datasets with thousands of samples and face very long runtimes or memory issues without clear guidance on when to avoid them.

### Why it matters
New users frequently misuse `LeaveOneOut()` on large data, leading to poor experience. The current recommendation to use `KFold` or `ShuffleSplit` exists but is not prominent enough.

### Proposed Improvement

- Add a clearer `UserWarning` when `n_samples` is large (e.g., > 1000 for `LeaveOneOut`).
- Improve the docstring with stronger recommendations and a short note about computational complexity.
- Add a small example showing when to prefer `KFold` instead.

**Location**:
`sklearn/model_selection/_split.py` → `class LeaveOneOut` and `class LeavePOut`

I have read the contributing guidelines and would like to work on this documentation improvement once the issue is triaged and approved.

Is this suitable for a first-time contributor?

records.title: DOC: Modernize and improve examples in train_test_split
records.body:
### Current Problem

The examples in `train_test_split` (`sklearn/model_selection/_split.py`) mix old NumPy-style output with pandas DataFrames, but the pandas part is not very clear or modern.

Many new users expect to see how the function behaves with DataFrames (column names and index are preserved, etc.).

### Why it matters
`train_test_split` is one of the most commonly used functions in scikit-learn. Clear, modern examples help users understand the expected behavior, especially when working with pandas DataFrames.

### Proposed Improvement

- Update the pandas example to clearly show that column names and index are preserved in the output.
- Add one short example demonstrating the `stratify` parameter.
- Make the output more readable and consistent.

**Location**:
`sklearn/model_selection/_split.py` → `train_test_split` function (Examples section)

I have read the contributing guidelines and would like to work on this documentation improvement once the issue is triaged and approved.

records.title: MAINT: Improve array API consistency in _validate_shuffle_split
records.body:
### Current Problem

The helper function `_validate_shuffle_split` (used by `train_test_split`, `ShuffleSplit`, `StratifiedShuffleSplit`, etc.) still uses NumPy-specific patterns (`np.asarray`, `.dtype.kind`, etc.).

Other parts of the same file (`StratifiedKFold`, `StratifiedShuffleSplit`, etc.) have already been updated to support the Array API using `get_namespace` and `move_to`.

This creates inconsistency inside `_split.py`.

### Why it matters
scikit-learn is actively improving Array API support across the library. Small inconsistencies make future maintenance harder and limit compatibility with non-NumPy arrays (such as CuPy).

### Proposed Improvement

Make `_validate_shuffle_split` more consistent with the rest of the module by:
- Using `get_namespace` where appropriate
- Handling array API inputs gracefully while keeping the current NumPy behavior unchanged

**Location**:
`sklearn/model_selection/_split.py` → `_validate_shuffle_split` function

I have read the contributing guidelines and would like to work on this small maintenance task once the issue is triaged.

records.title: TST: Add edge-case tests for StratifiedGroupKFold
records.body:
### Current Problem

`StratifiedGroupKFold` has complex logic in `_iter_test_indices` and `_find_best_fold`.
There are several corner cases (e.g. groups with only one sample, very uneven class distributions, or small number of groups) that can lead to unexpected behavior or degenerate splits.

Current test coverage for these edge cases is limited.

### Proposed Improvement

Add targeted tests in `sklearn/model_selection/tests/test_split.py` for:

- Each group containing only one sample
- One class appearing in only one group
- `shuffle=True` with a small number of groups
- Cases where `n_splits` is close to the number of groups

This will help prevent regressions and increase confidence in the implementation.

**Location**:
`sklearn/model_selection/_split.py` (class `StratifiedGroupKFold`) + corresponding tests in `test_split.py`

I have already opened a few documentation issues. I would like to work on adding these tests once this issue is triaged.

Is this suitable for a new contributor?

records.title: [BUG] BayesianRidge.predict with return_std=True fails to center test features, leading to incorrect predictive variance
records.body: ### Describe the bug and give evidence about its user-facing impact In `BayesianRidge`, the predictive variance calculation in the `predict` method is mathematically inconsistent with the training process when `fit_intercept=True` (the default). During `fit()`, the model centers the features (`X - X_offset_`), but during `predict()`, the variance is calculated using the **raw** test features `X_test` instead of centering them by the training mean `X_offset_`. As a result, the model reports its lowest uncertainty at the coordinate origin rather than at the center of the training data. For datasets far from the origin, this leads to significantly wrong uncertainty estimation, violating the principle that a Bayesian model should be most certain in the region where it has observed the most data. #### Mathematical formulation The original problem is $y = w^T x + b + \epsilon$. Instead, scikit-learn solves a centered version $y = w^T \tilde{x} + b' + \epsilon$, where $\tilde{x} = x - E[x]$, in order to find $w$ and $b'$, and finally $b$ is computed as $b = b' - w^T E[x]$. First, $b'$ is estimated using a frequentist approach (OLS/MLE) to be $b' = E[y]$, since $E[\tilde{x}] = 0$. This allows the problem to be reduced to $\tilde{y} = y - b' = w^T \tilde{x} + \epsilon$, on which a Bayesian approach is used to find $w$ (the posterior mean). After $w$ is found, the predictive distribution of $\tilde{y}$ on a new test point $\tilde{x}$ is then given by $$\tilde{\mu} = w^T \tilde{x}$$ $$\sigma^2 = \alpha^{-1} + \tilde{x}^T \Sigma_w \tilde{x}$$ But since $y = \tilde{y} + b'$, the predictive distribution of $y$ has the mean shifted to $$\mu = w^T \tilde{x} + b'$$ while the variance stays the same. However, our test point is actually $x$, so this all becomes $$\mu = w^T (x - \mu_x) + b' = w^T x + b$$ $$\sigma^2 = \alpha^{-1} + (x - \mu_x)^T \Sigma_w (x - \mu_x)$$ where $\mu_x = E[x]$ (estimated using the training data). Note that `predict` returns `y_mean` and `y_std`, where `y_mean` is exactly $\mu$, but `y_std` is not $\sigma$; instead it is $$\alpha^{-1} + x^T \Sigma_w x$$ What is missing is to subtract $\mu_x$ from $x$ before the variance computation. ### Steps/Code to Reproduce ```python import numpy as np import matplotlib.pyplot as plt from sklearn.linear_model import BayesianRidge n = 4 x_train = np.linspace(80, 100, n) y_train = x_train + 10*np.random.RandomState(0).standard_normal(n) model = BayesianRidge().fit(x_train.reshape(-1, 1), y_train) x = np.linspace(-100, 100, 101) y_mean, y_std = model.predict(x.reshape(-1, 1), return_std=True) print(f"Std (x={x[50]:3g}): {y_std[50]:7.4f}") print(f"Std (x={x[-1]:3g}): {y_std[-1]:7.4f}") plt.plot(x_train, y_train, 'r.') plt.plot(x, y_mean, 'b-') plt.fill_between(x, y_mean - y_std, y_mean + y_std, color='RoyalBlue') plt.title('Actual Results') plt.show() x_train = np.linspace(80, 100, n) x_train -= x_train.mean() y_train = x_train + 10*np.random.RandomState(0).standard_normal(n) model = BayesianRidge().fit(x_train.reshape(-1, 1), y_train) x = np.linspace(-100, 100, 101) y_mean, y_std = model.predict(x.reshape(-1, 1), return_std=True) print(f"Std (x={x[50]:3g}): {y_std[50]:7.4f}") print(f"Std (x={x[-1]:3g}): {y_std[-1]:7.4f}") plt.plot(x_train, y_train, 'r.') plt.plot(x, y_mean, 'b-') plt.fill_between(x, y_mean - y_std, y_mean + y_std, color='RoyalBlue') plt.title('Correct when data is already centered') plt.show() x_train = np.linspace(80, 100, n) y_train = x_train + 10*np.random.RandomState(0).standard_normal(n) model = BayesianRidge().fit(x_train.reshape(-1, 1), y_train) x = np.linspace(-100, 100, 101) y_mean = model.predict(x.reshape(-1, 1)) _, y_std = model.predict((x - model.X_offset_).reshape(-1, 1), return_std=True) print(f"Std (x={x[50]:3g}): {y_std[50]:7.4f}") print(f"Std (x={x[-1]:3g}): {y_std[-1]:7.4f}") plt.plot(x_train, y_train, 'r.') plt.plot(x, y_mean, 'b-') plt.fill_between(x, y_mean - y_std, y_mean + y_std, color='RoyalBlue') plt.title('Expected Results') plt.show() ``` ### Expected Results Lowest variance close to the training data. ### Actual Results Lowest variance close to the origin. records.title: Support for building against a SciPy which uses ILP64 BLAS and `cython_blas`
records.body:
Hi all, this issue is to propose adding support for building scikit-learn against a SciPy install that was built with ILP64 (i.e., 64-bit integers rather than the default LP64 / 32-bit integers - see https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/64-bit_computing#64-bit_data_models).

### Context

SciPy has wanted to have solid/full ILP64  support for years (efforts going back to 2020, and feature requests before that), because there are use cases and algorithms where support for large arrays where array indices don't fit in plain `int`'s is desirable. In the next SciPy release, 1.18.0, this will finally be arriving.

When building from source, there will actually be three builld modes:
1. LP64-only (default)
2. ILP64-only (opt-in with `-Duse-ilp64=true`)
3. ILP64 for all SciPy internals, but LP64 for `linalg.blas` and `linalg.cython_blas` low-level interfaces  (opt-in with `-Duse-ilp64=true -Dcython-blas-abi=lp64`)

See https://scipy.github.io/devdocs/building/blas_lapack.html#bit-integer-ilp64-blas-lapack for details.

Wheels on PyPI will continue to be LP64-only, so the ABI of `cython_blas` and `cython_lapack` won't be broken. However, when building from source, ILP64 can be chosen - and going ILP64-only means that downstream users of `scipy.linalg.blas|lapack|cython_blas|cython_lapack` need to work with that change.

Mode (3) can be useful as a transition mechanism for adopters (and wouldn't affect scikit-learn), but mode (2) is probably preferred.

### Proposed solution

It is possible for scikit-learn and other downstream users to detect how SciPy was built, and adapt automatically - no new build flag will be needed in scikit-learn, it should "just work". Essentially, `scipy.linalg.cython_blas` will expose a `blas_int` that can be used. It's also not too difficult to use that conditionally when it exists, and fall back to plain `int` otherwise.

Then, there are two ways scikit-learn can go for its own Cython code:

1. Handle the change in [sklearn/utils/_cython_blas.pyx](https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/blob/main/sklearn/utils/_cython_blas.pyx) with a small shim in each function, and keep [sklearn/utils/_cython_blas.pxd](https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/blob/main/sklearn/utils/_cython_blas.pxd) unchanged.
2. Change `_cython_blas.pxd` as well to use `blas_int`, meaning all consumers of that interface (~15 files currently) need to be adapted as well.

It's not an either/or. Option 1 is a very localized change, and should probably be done either way. Option 2 can always be done later - it has the benefit of actually enabling use of large arrays with scikit-learn APIs as well (option 1 doesn't, because `_cython_blas.pxd` still uses `int`). So it depends on whether there's a benefit in doing that.

### Next step

I plan to open a PR for (1) soon. This is fairly well-tested now (https://github.com/rgommers/pixi-sklearn-ilp64), and we are adding a test package to SciPy CI that closely mirrors scikit-learn's `_cython_blas` wrappers. Also, we now have a regression test for Cython ABI/signature changes, so that should be fine now.

If you prefer to do (2), I'd be happy to work on that as well.

records.title: DOC: Add explicit mathematical formula for biased standard deviation in StandardScaler
records.body:
### Describe the issue linked to the documentation

The `StandardScaler` API reference says it Standardize features by removing the mean and scaling to unit variance and mentions `numpy.std(ddof=0)` in the "Notes" section, but does not explicitly state a mathematical equation.

For users with a statistical or mathematical background, it may be less transparent to rely on the documentation details of a third party library like NumPy than to provide a formal mathematical definition, which is easy to interpret as the difference between biased and unbiased estimators may not be immediately obvious to all users.

### Suggest a potential alternative/fix

I propose adding the explicit LaTeX formulas for the $z$-score and the standard deviation to the "Notes" section of the `StandardScaler` docstring. This clarifies the use of the biased estimator (division by $n$) versus the unbiased estimator (also known as Bessel's correction, $n-1$), which might be a point of confusion for users.

I propose rewriting Notes as:

We use a biased estimator for the standard deviation, equivalent to ``numpy.std(x, ddof=0)``, that is:

.. math::

    s = \sqrt{\frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^{n} (x_i - \mu)^2}



I’d be happy to submit a PR if this approach looks good.

records.title: ENH: Add confusion_matrix_diff to compare multiple models against a baseline
records.body:
> [!WARNING]
> This issue is not yet ready for a PR. If you are interested in contributing to scikit-learn, please have a look at our [contributing guidelines](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html), and in particular the sections for [new contributors](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#new-contributors) and the ["Needs triage"](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#issues-tagged-needs-triage) label.

### Describe the workflow you want to enable

When comparing classification models, users frequently need to understand how one model differs from another on a per-class basis. The current workflow requires manually computing separate confusion matrices and subtracting them:

```
cm1 = confusion_matrix(y_true, y_pred_baseline)
cm2 = confusion_matrix(y_true, y_pred_model2)
diff = cm2 - cm1
```

This pattern has no built-in support in sklearn and becomes error-prone when normalization is involved - normalizing before vs after subtraction gives different results and users may not be aware of this distinction.

There is also no standard scalable way to compare multiple models against a single baseline in one call.

### Describe your proposed solution

Add confusion_matrix_diff to sklearn.metrics with the following signature:

```
def confusion_matrix_diff(
    y_true_or_cm_baseline,
    *args,
    precomputed=False,
    labels=None,
    sample_weight=None,
    normalize=None
)
```

**Label mode (precomputed=False):**

```
# Two models
result = confusion_matrix_diff(y_true, y_pred_baseline, y_pred2)

# Three models
result = confusion_matrix_diff(y_true, y_pred_baseline, y_pred2, y_pred3)

# With normalization
result = confusion_matrix_diff(y_true, y_pred_baseline, y_pred2, normalize='true')
```

**Precomputed mode (precomputed=True):**

`result = confusion_matrix_diff(cm_baseline, cm2, cm3, precomputed=True)`

Returns a 3D array of shape (n_comparisons, n_classes, n_classes) where:
- Positive values = comparison model better than baseline
- Negative values = baseline better than comparison model

The normalize parameter mirrors confusion_matrix exactly - normalization is applied to each matrix individually before subtraction, giving meaningful per-class rate differences rather than raw count differences.

### Describe alternatives you've considered, if relevant

Users can subtract confusion matrices manually, but this does not handle:
- Consistent normalization across matrices before subtraction
- Multi-model comparison in a single call
- Input validation for mismatched label sets or matrix shapes

A utility function makes this discoverable, correct by default, and consistent with the existing confusion_matrix API.

### Additional context

### Describe the bug and give evidence about its user-facing impact

The logic for array API was recently modified to allow 'y' inputs of a potentially different type than 'X', particularly when it comes to classifiers where 'y' might be strings.

But it appears this logic does not always work when `y` is a pandas object, or at least doesn't work for all methods.

ys = pd.Series(y)

records.title: _MPLTreeExporter: ValueError when using custom colors
records.body:
### Describe the bug and give evidence about its user-facing impact

When using _MPLTreeExporter with custom class colors, valid RGB triplets can be turned into invalid Matplotlib color strings if one of the RGB components is `0`.

I found this while preparing teaching/presentation material and trying to make a decision tree use the same class colors as other plots in the same figure.

### Steps/Code to Reproduce

```python
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from sklearn.datasets import load_iris
from sklearn.tree import DecisionTreeClassifier
from sklearn.tree._export import _MPLTreeExporter


iris = load_iris()
X = iris.data[:, :2]
y = iris.target

clf = DecisionTreeClassifier(max_depth=3, random_state=42)
clf.fit(X, y)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(10, 6))
exporter = _MPLTreeExporter(
    feature_names=iris.feature_names[:2],
    class_names=iris.target_names,
    filled=True,
    impurity=False,
    node_ids=False,
    proportion=False,
)
exporter.colors["rgb"] = [
    # Use colors with zero components to trigger the bug
    [0, 255, 255],
    [255, 0, 255],
    [255, 255, 0],
]
exporter.export(clf, ax=ax)

# ValueError: Invalid RGBA argument: '# 0ffff'

records.title: BUG Spurious UserWarning with the deprecation of penalty in LogisticRegression
records.body:
When running this minimal example:

```python
import numpy as np
from sklearn.datasets import make_classification
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression

X, y = make_classification(random_state=0)
log_reg = LogisticRegression(penalty=None).fit(X, y)
```

we get the following deprecation warning:

```
[/Users/glemaitre/Documents/packages/python-stack/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/sklearn/linear_model/_logistic.py:1135](http://localhost:8888/Users/glemaitre/Documents/packages/python-stack/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/sklearn/linear_model/_logistic.py#line=1134): FutureWarning: 'penalty' was deprecated in version 1.8 and will be removed in 1.10. To avoid this warning, leave 'penalty' set to its default value and use 'l1_ratio' or 'C' instead. Use l1_ratio=0 instead of penalty='l2', l1_ratio=1 instead of penalty='l1', and C=np.inf instead of penalty=None.
```

which is completely fine. In my case, I wanted an unpenalized model and thus fix `C=np.inf`:

```python
import numpy as np
from sklearn.datasets import make_classification
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression

X, y = make_classification(random_state=0)
log_reg = LogisticRegression(C=np.inf).fit(X, y)
```

and I get the following warning:

```
[/Users/glemaitre/Documents/packages/python-stack/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/sklearn/linear_model/_logistic.py:1170](http://localhost:8888/Users/glemaitre/Documents/packages/python-stack/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/sklearn/linear_model/_logistic.py#line=1169): UserWarning: Setting penalty=None will ignore the C and l1_ratio parameters
```

I think that this warning is spurious. We probably set the `penalty` internally which trigger this warning.

records.title: BUG _parallel_pairwise does not slice Y_norm_squared alongside Y when n_jobs > 1
records.body:
### Describe the bug and give evidence about its user-facing impact

`_parallel_pairwise` chunks `Y` into slices for parallel execution but passes `**kwds` (including `Y_norm_squared`) unchanged. When `euclidean_distances` is called with `Y_norm_squared` and `n_jobs > 1`, this causes a `ValueError` due to shape mismatch between the sliced `Y` and the full `Y_norm_squared`.

### Steps/Code to Reproduce

```python
from sklearn.metrics.pairwise import _parallel_pairwise, euclidean_distances
import numpy as np

X = np.random.RandomState(42).rand(13, 4)
Y_norm_squared = np.sum(X ** 2, axis=1)

# n_jobs=1: no chunking, Y_norm_squared matches Y — works fine
result = _parallel_pairwise(X, X, euclidean_distances, n_jobs=1, Y_norm_squared=Y_norm_squared)
print("n_jobs=1: OK", result.shape)

# n_jobs=2: Y chunked but Y_norm_squared stays full — crashes
_parallel_pairwise(X, X, euclidean_distances, n_jobs=2, Y_norm_squared=Y_norm_squared)
```

### Expected Results

No error is thrown. The `n_jobs=2` call returns the same distance matrix as `n_jobs=1`.

### Actual Results

```python-traceback
ValueError: Incompatible dimensions for Y of shape (6, 4) and Y_norm_squared of shape (13,).
```

### Versions

```
System:
    python: 3.12.9 | packaged by Anaconda, Inc. | (main, Feb  6 2025, 12:55:12) [Clang 14.0.6 ]
   machine: macOS-26.4.1-arm64-arm-64bit

Python dependencies:
      sklearn: 1.8.0
          pip: 25.0

       Cython: 3.2.4
       pandas: 2.3.3
   matplotlib: None
       joblib: 1.5.3
threadpoolctl: 3.6.0

Built with OpenMP: True
```

Also confirmed on `main` (the code at `sklearn/metrics/pairwise.py` line 1986 still passes `**kwds` unsliced).

### Interest in fixing the bug

Yes — I have a fix ready in #33876. The fix slices `Y_norm_squared` alongside `Y` in the `Parallel` call inside `_parallel_pairwise()`.

records.title: Add 'quantile' strategy to `calibration_curve`
records.body:
### Describe the workflow you want to enable

Choose between different binning strategies ("uniform" fixed width bins, "quantile" equal mass bins) to estimate the calibration curve.

### Describe your proposed solution

Adding in `calibration_curve` a new `strategy = "uniform"` or `strategy = "quantile"` option to switch between the two binning strategies. We can for now just add the option and change the default in a follow up PR.

We can also add (in the same or follow up PR) the `strategy="isotonic"`  option to implement the CORP approach as advocated in #23132.

### Describe alternatives you've considered, if relevant

_No response_

### Additional context

There are multiple issues / PRs on implementing calibration metrics (for example the expected calibration error, the Brier score decomposition) and improving reliability diagrams:
#18268, #11096,  #22233, #21774, #23767,  #23132

There are two main ways to estimate the calibration curve (and metrics):
1. using binning, either "uniform" (fixed-width bins) or "quantile" (equal mass bins)
2. using isotonic regression, this is the [CORP](https://arxiv.org/abs/2008.03033) approach, see #23132

For the binning case, the quality of the estimate in the binning depends crucially on
1a. the number of bins, it seems that `n_bins=n**(1/3)` is best, this is tackled by #33856
1b. the binning strategy, it seems that "quantile" is better, see [Roelofs et al](https://arxiv.org/abs/2012.08668) or [Nixon et al](https://arxiv.org/abs/1904.01685)

Reading through the literature, I feel that the "best estimator for the calibration curve/metrics" is not yet settled.   Based on the experiments reported in the [CORP](https://arxiv.org/abs/2008.03033) paper, the isotonic regression seems the most accurate. However there are ways to debias the binned estimates for the Brier score decomposition that we could investigate, see [Ferro and Fricker, 2012](https://empslocal.ex.ac.uk/people/staff/ferro/Publications/ferro-fricker2012copyright.pdf).

Also, we might want the different options with each its own benefits: fixed-width bins to visually compare different curves or put them in a dataframe, equal mass bins to get a more reliable curve with a manageable length (`n_bins = n**(1/3)`), isotonic regression for its accuracy but at the expense of  a crowded curve (length `n`).

Overall, having the different options seems to me the best way for further implementations of the calibration metrics or curve, without having to commit to one option over another.

cc @ogrisel @lorentzenchr

### Describe the bug and give evidence about its user-facing impact

KMeans does not produce expected centers update after 1 iteration.

Context: I was trying to use sklearn as a reference to debug a custom kmeans implementation and found this unexpected behavior.

### Steps/Code to Reproduce

With `sample_weights = np.ones(...)`, I'd expect `weight_in_clusters[i] == np.sum(labels == i)`, but it's not the case.

Run with `OMP_NUM_THREADS=1`:

```python
import zipfile

import numpy as np
from sklearn.cluster._k_means_lloyd import lloyd_iter_chunked_dense
from sklearn.utils._openmp_helpers import _openmp_effective_n_threads

with zipfile.ZipFile("data.zip", "r") as zip_ref:
    zip_ref.extractall("data")


X = np.load("data/X.npy")
centers = np.load("data/centers.npy")
sample_weight = np.ones_like(X[..., 0])

K = centers.shape[0]

centers_new = np.zeros_like(centers)
labels = np.full(X.shape[0], -1, dtype=np.int32)
weight_in_clusters = np.zeros(K, dtype=X.dtype)
center_shift = np.zeros(K, dtype=X.dtype)

n_threads = _openmp_effective_n_threads()


lloyd_iter_chunked_dense(
    X,
    sample_weight,
    centers,
    centers_new,
    weight_in_clusters,
    labels,
    center_shift,
    n_threads,
)
print("weight in cluster #996", weight_in_clusters[996])
print("# of assignments to cluster #996", np.sum(labels == 996))

print(
    "expected new cluster #996",
    np.sum(X[labels == 996], axis=0) / np.sum(labels == 996),
)
print("sklearn new cluster #996", centers_new[996])

### Describe the issue linked to the documentation

Some error messages in sklearn.utils.validation are very brief and may not provide enough guidance to users.

For example, messages like "Input contains NaN" could be expanded to suggest possible fixes such as handling missing values before passing data to estimators.

I would like to improve the clarity of one such error message to make it more helpful for users.

### Suggest a potential alternative/fix

Improve the wording of existing error messages in validation utilities to provide clearer guidance to users.

For example, instead of a short message like:
"Input contains NaN"

it could be expanded to:
"Input contains NaN values. Please handle missing values (e.g., imputation or removal) before passing data to the estimator."

This change would not affect functionality but would improve usability and reduce confusion for users encountering these errors.

records.title: Make `_array_api_for_tests` accept a `dtype_name` and raise `SkipTest` if the requested dtype/device is not supported
records.body:
As discussed in #32460, the supported dtype can sometimes vary even if the device name is the same, and we need to do runtime inspection for instance using `__array_namespace_info__.dtypes`. It means that we would need to update all the array API test to pass both `device` and `dtype_name` to `_array_api_for_tests` to do this check and raise `SkipTest` when appropriate instead of running a test that will fail with a low level error message.

This is the case for PyTorch with the XPU device on different kinds of hardware: some Intel GPUs reachable via this device do support the `xp.float64` dtype while others don't.

I think @cakedev0 has access to such hardware on his laptop.

records.title: `partial_fit` for `Ridge`
records.body:
### Describe the workflow you want to enable

The `Ridge` family is already compatible with the Array API, which is great for pytorch compatibility! It simplifies linear probing evaluations for foundation models.

However, these models often use datasets with many examples.
It is not always feasible to accumulate features in memory before passing them to a ridge classifier.

It would be nice if `Ridge` had a `partial_fit` method which allowed processing the dataset in batches.
With $D$ features and $N$ examples, `Ridge` would only accumulate the features statistics ($D \times D$) instead of all the features ($N \times D$)

### Describe your proposed solution

We accumulate the sufficient statistics $A = X^\top X \in \mathbb{R}^{D \times D}$ and $B = X^\top Y \in \mathbb{R}^{D \times C}$, both of size independent of $N$. The closed-form ridge solution is $W = (A + \lambda I)^{-1} B$. Because $X$ is never materialized, memory is $O(D^2)$ instead of $O(ND)$, so the probe scales to arbitrarily large train sets.


### Describe alternatives you've considered, if relevant

Implement it outside of scikit learn: https://github.com/braindecode/OpenEEGBench/blob/ede655f1294feef15ff6be4d6e6d94628ab9187e/open_eeg_bench/ridge_probe.py#L79-L273
Then add a test for consistency with the scikit learn pipeline on a small random datasets: https://github.com/braindecode/OpenEEGBench/blob/ede655f1294feef15ff6be4d6e6d94628ab9187e/tests/test_ridge_probe.py#L42-L99

### Additional context

We are using this for [OpenEEGBench](https://github.com/braindecode/OpenEEGBench), a library for benchmarking EEG foundation models.

Context: https://github.com/braindecode/OpenEEGBench/pull/32#discussion_r3172514283

Having to go to https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/array_api.html#support-for-array-api-compatible-inputs is possible but a bit tedious.

Until today I was thinking that we don't need this because "all estimators will support array API input, even if it doesn't make them faster". Which removes the need to explicitly list it on each estimator's page.

What do others think about this?

records.title: PERF: Avoid unnecessary n_samples x n_samples diagonal sparse matrix in `_rescale_data`
records.body:
> [!WARNING]
> This issue is not yet ready for a PR. If you are interested in contributing to scikit-learn, please have a look at our [contributing guidelines](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html), and in particular the sections for [new contributors](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#new-contributors) and the ["Needs triage"](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#issues-tagged-needs-triage) label.

### Describe the workflow you want to enable

When fitting any linear model (e.g. `LinearRegression`, `Ridge`, `ElasticNet`) on sparse data
with `sample_weight`, the internal function `_rescale_data` is called to bake sample weights
into the data before solving. Currently it constructs an intermediate `(n_samples x n_samples)`
diagonal sparse matrix just to perform a simple row scaling, then runs a full sparse matrix
multiply through `safe_sparse_dot`.

For large sparse datasets this creates unnecessary memory allocation and computation on every
`fit()` call. The issue affects all linear models that support `sample_weight` with sparse input.

### Describe your proposed solution

Replace the `dia_array` + `safe_sparse_dot` approach with a direct elementwise row-scaling via
`csr_array.multiply()`, which is built for this exact operation and needs no intermediate matrix.

**Current code** in `sklearn/linear_model/_base.py:252`:

```python
if sp.issparse(X) or sp.issparse(y):
    sw_matrix = sparse.dia_array(
        (sample_weight_sqrt, 0), shape=(n_samples, n_samples)
    )

if sp.issparse(X):
    X = safe_sparse_dot(sw_matrix, X)

if sp.issparse(y):
    y = safe_sparse_dot(sw_matrix, y)
```

**Proposed code:**

```python
if sp.issparse(X):
    X = X.multiply(sample_weight_sqrt[:, None])

if sp.issparse(y):
    sw = sample_weight_sqrt[:, None] if y.ndim > 1 else sample_weight_sqrt
    y = y.multiply(sw)
```

Both produce identical results — verified against the existing `test_rescale_data` test and
directly against the old implementation across all input combinations.

**Why it is better:**

- Eliminates the `(n_samples x n_samples)` diagonal sparse matrix allocation entirely
- `csr_array.multiply(vector)` is O(nnz) with no intermediate object;
  `dia_array @ csr_array` constructs the diagonal object first, then runs a matrix-multiply
  code path
- For 100k samples: old code allocates a 100k-element `data` array and shape tuple for the
  `dia_array` before touching `X`; new code works directly on the `nnz` non-zero entries

## Describe alternatives you've considered

- `scipy.sparse.diags(sample_weight_sqrt) @ X` — same problem, still builds an intermediate
  diagonal sparse matrix
- Keeping `safe_sparse_dot` — unnecessary here since `.multiply()` handles elementwise
  scaling natively and always returns a sparse result

## Additional context

- **Affected function:** `sklearn.linear_model._base._rescale_data` (line 220)
- **Affected models:** all linear models that accept `sample_weight` with sparse `X` —
  `LinearRegression`, `Ridge`, `ElasticNet`, `Lasso`, and their CV variants
- **Tests:** the existing `test_rescale_data` in `sklearn/linear_model/tests/test_base.py`
  already covers `sparse_container x n_targets` combinations — no new test infrastructure needed
- **Fix is ready:** branch `perf/avoid-dia-array-in-rescale-data` on fork

## Labels

`Enhancement`, `Needs Triage`, `module:linear_model`

records.title: [FEA] Add Ambiguity Range metric for safety-critical classification
records.body: > [!WARNING] > This issue is not yet ready for a PR. If you are interested in contributing to scikit-learn, please have a look at our [contributing guidelines](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html), and in particular the sections for [new contributors](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#new-contributors) and the ["Needs triage"](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#issues-tagged-needs-triage) label. ### Describe the workflow you want to enable Practitioners in safety-critical fields—such as medical diagnostics, structural engineering, or high-stakes financial modeling—require a method to explicitly quantify the "Indecision Zone" of a binary classifier. While aggregate metrics like the F1-score or Area Under the ROC Curve (AUC) provide a high-level view of model performance, they often mask the specific regions where a model's prediction is statistically equivalent to guessing. By implementing the ambiguity_range_score, we enable a Tri-Modal Decision Workflow: Automated Action (High Confidence): Samples with scores above the Upper Threshold ($T_{upper}$, representing 100% Precision) or below the Lower Threshold ($T_{lower}$, representing 100% Recall) are handled automatically by the system with high trust. Human-in-the-Loop (Ambiguity Zone): Samples falling within the range $\mathcal{A} = T_{upper} - T_{lower}$ are flagged for manual expert review. Reliability Benchmarking: This allows developers to select models that minimize required human intervention by reducing the Ambiguity Range, even in cases where traditional metrics like AUC remain static. Safety-Critical Calibration: Practitioners can visualize exactly how much of a population falls into a "Gray Zone" where the model cannot guarantee a certain outcome. ### Describe your proposed solution I propose adding a new metric: ambiguity_range_score(y_true, y_score, *, epsilon=0.0, pos_label=None). Key Technical Implementations: The Ambiguity Measure ($\mathcal{A}$): Defined as the difference between the threshold required for perfect precision and the threshold required for perfect recall. Epsilon ($\epsilon$) Robustness: To handle real-world datasets containing outliers or label noise, the epsilon parameter allows for a "Soft Ambiguity" measure (e.g., $\epsilon=0.01$ for 99% precision/recall). This prevents a single mislabeled data point from artificially maximizing the range to 1.0. Integration: The function utilizes the existing precision_recall_curve logic to find the critical boundary points, ensuring consistency with scikit-learn’s internal API. ### Threshold Independence & Model Robustness A common limitation of standard classification metrics is their dependence on an arbitrary decision threshold (e.g., 0.5). Choosing a single threshold is often a heuristic choice made during deployment that may not reflect the inherent separability of the model. The ambiguity_range_score is superior in this regard because it is threshold-independent. Rather than evaluating performance at a single point, it quantifies the "Indecision Zone" as a global characteristic of the model's feature-space quality. By measuring the distance between the two extreme bounds of reliability ($T_{upper}$ and $T_{lower}$), it provides a scalar value that describes model "resoluteness" regardless of where an individual user might eventually set their operating point. ### Describe alternatives you've considered, if relevant I have considered using the Detection Error Tradeoff (DET) curve; however, while DET curves are excellent for visual analysis, they do not provide a direct, scalar "range" value that can be easily used for automated model selection or as a clear KPI for "Human-in-the-Loop" resource planning. ### Additional context I have attached a figure that provides an empirical verification of the metric: Distribution Density Plot: Illustrates the score overlapping that generates the Ambiguity Range ($\mathcal{A}$) and the resulting Ternary Decision Logic. Sensitivity Analysis: Demonstrates how the metric responds to increasing Label Noise vs. Feature Noise, and confirms that the epsilon parameter successfully maintains metric robustness in noisy environments. Developed and proposed by Kian Maleki. Here is the proposed implementation for `ambiguity_range_score`: ```python import numpy as np from sklearn.utils import check_consistent_length from sklearn.metrics import precision_recall_curve def ambiguity_range_score(y_true, y_score, *, epsilon=0.0, pos_label=None): """Compute the Ambiguity Measure between perfect precision and recall. The Ambiguity Measure is the difference between the threshold required for perfect precision and the threshold required for perfect recall. Parameters ---------- y_true : array-like of shape (n_samples,) True binary labels. y_score : array-like of shape (n_samples,) Target scores, can either be probability estimates of the positive class or confidence values. epsilon : float, default=0.0 The tolerance for "perfect" metrics. (e.g., 0.01 for 99% precision/recall). pos_label : int, float, bool or str, default=None The label of the positive class. Returns ------- ambiguity : float The calculated range between thresholds. A smaller value indicates better class separability. """ check_consistent_length(y_true, y_score) # Calculate Precision-Recall curve and thresholds precision, recall, thresholds = precision_recall_curve( y_true, y_score, pos_label=pos_label ) # 1. Upper Threshold: Minimum score where Precision >= 1 - epsilon target_p = 1.0 - epsilon p_indices = np.where(precision >= target_p)[0] # Clip index for thresholds t_upper = thresholds[p_indices[0]] if p_indices.size > 0 else np.max(y_score) # 2. Lower Threshold: Maximum score where Recall >= 1 - epsilon target_r = 1.0 - epsilon r_indices = np.where(recall >= target_r)[0] t_lower = thresholds[r_indices[-1]] if r_indices.size > 0 else np.min(y_score) # 3. Ambiguity Measure return float(t_upper - t_lower) # Example Usage: if __name__ == "__main__": y_true = np.array([0, 0, 1, 1]) y_scores = np.array([0.1, 0.4, 0.35, 0.8]) print(f"Ambiguity Measure: {ambiguity_range_score(y_true, y_scores)}")

records.title: CountVectorizer fails when dealing with short strings and ngram_range > len of the strings
records.body:
### Describe the bug and give evidence about its user-facing impact

I was debugging a problem with the skrub GapEncoder in https://github.com/skrub-data/skrub/issues/770, and I realized that the root of the problem is somewhere in the CountVectorizer, specifically when it receives a column that includes only strings of length 1 (`"A"`).

After tracking down the problem, my understanding is that the CountVectorizer is failing because all strings in the column are shorter than the minimum value in `ngram_range` (see the example).

The result is the exception
```
ValueError: empty vocabulary; perhaps the documents only contain stop words
```

which is not giving me a lot of information to debug. I think the error message could be improved so that it describes the situation in more detail.

### Steps/Code to Reproduce

```python
import numpy as np
from sklearn.feature_extraction.text import CountVectorizer
import string

rng = np.random.default_rng()
letters = rng.choice(list(string.ascii_letters), 1000)

# works
CountVectorizer(analyzer="char", ).fit_transform(np.array(letters))
# raises ValueError: empty vocabulary; perhaps the documents only contain stop words
CountVectorizer(analyzer="char", ngram_range=(2,4)).fit_transform(np.array(letters))
```

### Expected Results

I think it makes sense that the exception is raised, so the current behavior is "expected". I would rather have a more informative error if possible, however. Something like "the vocabulary is empty because all values in the series are shorter than the minimum value of ngram_range".

records.title: Improve `pairwise_distances` so that it works with array API inputs for all supported metrics
records.body:
> [!WARNING]
> This issue is not yet ready for a PR. If you are interested in contributing to scikit-learn, please have a look at our [contributing guidelines](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html), and in particular the sections for [new contributors](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#new-contributors) and the ["Needs triage"](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#issues-tagged-needs-triage) label.

The `pairwise_distances` function can't always be called when using array API. We should fix this.

`pairwise_distances` with `metric="mahalanobis"` (and other scipy-delegated metrics not in `PAIRWISE_DISTANCE_FUNCTIONS`) does not work with array API inputs on non-CPU devices.

The `"mahalanobis"` metric is not in scikit-learn's `PAIRWISE_DISTANCE_FUNCTIONS`, so `pairwise_distances` falls through to the scipy fallback path, which calls `scipy.spatial.distance.cdist` / `scipy.spatial.distance.pdist`. As of scipy 1.17.1, both functions call `np.asarray()` on their inputs, which fails for GPU tensors (e.g. PyTorch MPS/CUDA, CuPy).

I'm not sure if the solution for this is to implement this in scikit-learn or wait for scipy to add support for it. For other metrics we have implementations in Python in `sklearn/metrics/pairwise.py`, so maybe there is no performance downside to having a Python implementation? If yes, then this is "just" a question of turning the handle to implement new distances?

xref https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/pull/33573/changes#r3079594482

records.title: Use automatic chunk size in `ledoit_wolf_shrinkage` (and friends?)
records.body:
> [!WARNING]
> This issue is not yet ready for a PR. If you are interested in contributing to scikit-learn, please have a look at our [contributing guidelines](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html), and in particular the sections for [new contributors](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#new-contributors) and the ["Needs triage"](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#issues-tagged-needs-triage) label.

This issue is a tracker for the task of adding chunking to the computation in `ledoit_wolf_shrinkage` (`sklearn/covariance/_shrunk_covariance.py`).

For the CPU implementation chunking is already supported. For the array API path we currently perform no chunking. Bigger chunks are better for GPU devices (in terms of execution time), but they require more memory.

After investigating and benchmarking a bit, I am not sure what we should do. For "tall and skinny" datasets blocking doesn't matter. For wide datasets it limits how much additional memory is used for temporaries. With `n_features=20_000` you'd use something like 1.6GB of extra memory without blocking. However, the speedup (MPS over numpy) when using blocking is much smaller than if the MPS implementation runs without blocking. It can be  5x - 10x without blocking and only something like 2x faster if you use `block_size=1000` for MPS as well.

Numpy is also faster if you increase the block size. For example, `block_size=2000` seems to speed things up by roughly a factor two and still only uses a small amount of memory.

So I think we could increase the block size, even for Numpy. But I am not sure how we should decide the trade-off between speed up and memory. We could use a block size like 3000 for all namespaces/devices to get most of the speed up and avoid catastrophic "out of memory" exceptions. The user could then tune the block size if they knew that they have enough memory? But it feels like I just made up 3000, it could equally be 4000 or 2000 - I couldn't argue which of these is more correct/better.

Quoting @ogrisel's comment here to make it easy to find:

> I suspect that for CPU devices (e.g. NumPy), the optimal block size should be set that the sum of intermediate arrays stays in Level 3 CPU cache (typically a few megabytes on most modern CPUs).
>
> It should be possible to tell if a given device is CPU or not using something like `getattr(array, "__dlpack_device__", lambda: (1, 0))()[0] in (1, 3)`.

A suggestion is to switch to using `block_size="auto"` as the default (instead of 1000). This would allow us to use a different value for different devices (eg CPUs vs GPUs). Maybe we could even determine the "best" size based on the L3 cache size, but maybe this is making things too complicated.

xref https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/pull/33573/changes#r3028299959

### Describe the workflow you want to enable

I'm not sure if this has already been requested, but i haven't seen any discussion about this yet.

The `_parameter_constraint` attribute works for hyperparameter validation, but it can easily adapted to make hyperparameters available, and their ranges programatically accesible.

This would be great for any AutoML application that deals with hyperparameter optimization, since there would be an officially supported interface within which you can build the search space in which to optimize. To avoid making too many changes, we could expect this kind of workflows to filter parameters like `n_jobs`, `copy_X` or other internal parameters instead of making the distinction a the package level.

### Describe your proposed solution

I see 2 possible ways to implement this:
1. Rename all `_parameter_constraint` attributes to `parameter_constraint`, making it clear that it is publicly accesible, and add references to it across the documentation pages.
2. Provide a new public method that returns the values in `_parameter_constaints`, adding a reference to it in the various documentation pages.

### Describe alternatives you've considered, if relevant

Users can already access `_parameter_constraints`. The only issue is that it's a private method and not well documented (which i understand, since now it's only meant for internal parameter validation).
