records.title: Improve error message when a polars `LazyFrame` is passed to `check_array`
records.body:
### Describe the bug and give evidence about its user-facing impact

Passing a polars `LazyFrame` to `check_array` — e.g. the result of
`pl.scan_parquet(...)` without a final `.collect()` — produces an error that suggests
reshaping the input. Through an estimator (`StandardScaler().fit(lazy_frame)`) the
error is different but equally unhelpful: `ValueError: setting an array element with
a sequence.`. Neither message mentions the `LazyFrame` or the actionable fix, which
is to call `.collect()`. An eager `pl.DataFrame` works fine; only the lazy variant
fails, so this is easy to hit at the end of a polars `scan_*` pipeline and the
reshape advice sends the user in the wrong direction.

(Lazy-frame *support* was discussed in the narwhals adoption RFC #31049 and left
out of scope — the expression-API code path that would enable it was not favored,
and row order is undefined on a narwhals `LazyFrame`. This issue is only about
failing with a useful message.)

### Steps/Code to Reproduce

```python
import polars as pl
from sklearn.utils import check_array
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler

X_lazy = pl.LazyFrame({"a": [1.0, 2.0], "b": [3.0, 4.0]})

check_array(X_lazy)            # ValueError: Expected 2D array, got scalar array ...
StandardScaler().fit(X_lazy)   # ValueError: setting an array element with a sequence.
```

### Expected Results

An error that names the type and the fix, in the same spirit as the existing
`np.matrix` and sparse-input guards:

```
TypeError: A polars LazyFrame was passed, but lazy dataframes are not supported. Use '.collect()' to convert it to a polars DataFrame.
```

### Actual Results

```
ValueError: Expected 2D array, got scalar array instead:
array=naive plan: (run LazyFrame.explain(optimized=True) to see the optimized plan)

DF ["a", "b"]; PROJECT */2 COLUMNS.
Reshape your data either using array.reshape(-1, 1) if your data has a single feature or array.reshape(1, -1) if it contains a single sample.
```

Through an estimator instead of `check_array` directly:

```
ValueError: setting an array element with a sequence.
```

The `LazyFrame` is not recognized by the narwhals-based dataframe detection
(`nw.dependencies.is_into_dataframe` returns `False` for it) and falls through to
`np.asarray`, which wraps it as a 0-d object scalar — hence the misleading messages
with the stringified query plan in the middle.

### Versions

```shell
System:
    python: 3.13.5 | packaged by Anaconda, Inc. | (main, Jun 12 2025, 11:23:37) [Clang 14.0.6 ]
   machine: macOS-15.7.3-arm64-arm-64bit-Mach-O

Python dependencies:
      sklearn: 1.9.0
          pip: None
   setuptools: None
        numpy: 2.4.6
        scipy: 1.17.1
       Cython: None
       pandas: None
   matplotlib: None
       joblib: 1.5.3
threadpoolctl: 3.6.0
     narwhals: 2.22.1

Built with OpenMP: True
```

polars 1.41.2. Also reproduced on the `1.10.dev0` nightly wheel (current main).


### Interest in fixing the bug

Yes, I would like to work on a PR (I will wait for triage before opening it).

Root cause: `check_array` detects dataframes via
`nw.dependencies.is_into_dataframe` / `is_into_series`, both of which return
`False` for a `LazyFrame`, so it falls through to `np.asarray`, which wraps the
`LazyFrame` as a 0-d object scalar. The downstream dimension checks then produce
the misleading "scalar array" / "setting an array element with a sequence" errors.

Proposed fix: add an early guard in `check_array`, next to the narwhals dataframe
handling, using `narwhals.stable.v2.dependencies.is_polars_lazyframe` (available at
the current `narwhals>=2.0.1` floor), raising a `TypeError` that names the type and
suggests `.collect()`, following the wording style of the existing `np.matrix` and
sparse-input guards. The guard would be polars-specific: the generic
`is_into_lazyframe` helper is not available at the narwhals version floor, and the
`.collect()` advice is polars-specific anyway. I have this implemented locally with
tests and a changelog fragment.

records.title: Improve user experience with fetch_openml when md5 doesn't match
records.body:
### Describe the workflow you want to enable

When the md5 hash does not match in fetch_openml, the user has a hard time finding out how to move forward.

### Describe your proposed solution

Two possible improvements (both useful):
* In the error message, print the file name that is offending, and suggest to the user to remove it
* Have a retry option

records.title: Add an option to use Latin Hypercube Sampling to `RandomizedSearchCV` and `HalvingSearchCV`
records.body:
> [!WARNING]
> This issue is not yet ready for a PR. If you are interested in contributing to scikit-learn, please have a look at our [contributing guidelines](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html), and in particular the sections for [new contributors](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#new-contributors) and the ["Needs triage"](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#issues-tagged-needs-triage) label.

### Describe the workflow you want to enable

[Latin Hypercube Sampling ](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Latin_hypercube_sampling) is an alternative to uniform sampling that prevent clumping sampled values.

It was empirically shown to reduce the variance and improve the average result of randomized search by better covering the search space, in particular when running RS with a limited number of iterations on a medium to large dimensional parameters search space:

https://www.r-bloggers.com/2019/07/latin-hypercube-sampling-in-hyper-parameter-optimization/

### Describe your proposed solution

I think we could introduce a new `sampling_strategy = {"latin_hypercube", "uniform"}` parameter to the `RandomizedSearchCV` and `HalvingSearchCV` classes.

Implementing LHC sampling should be trivial for discretized search spaces and the extra code complexity should be very limited. For parameter ranges specified as `scipy.stats` distribution objects, it should be possible to map LHC samples from the 0-1 range to the actual param space using the inverse CDF functions.

### Additional context

Arguably, the linked blog post is not a proper peer reviewed paper, but I doubt that such a simple yet practically seemingly incremental improvement over RS has a chance of ever being published in a peer reviewed journal/conference and get a large enough citation count to meet our formal inclusion criteria.

Implementing a prototype and empirically evaluating it on a large and diverse enough set of HP tuning problems (varying hyper-parameter dimensionality, number of candidates, kinds of data and pipelines to ensure diversity of sensitivity of perf metric to hparam values...) could help us decide whether this option would be worthy of inclusion or not. Interested contributors, feel free to create a dedicated prototype notebook or repo and share the results as a comment to this issue.

records.title: Declare metadata properties to be used by the routers
records.body:
> [!WARNING]
> This issue is not yet ready for a PR. If you are interested in contributing to scikit-learn, please have a look at our [contributing guidelines](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html), and in particular the sections for [new contributors](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#new-contributors) and the ["Needs triage"](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#issues-tagged-needs-triage) label.

When working on https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/pull/34263, I realized that `Pipeline` may not be the only place where we need to specify metadata that needs to be transformed like `X`.

There are several estimators that transform `X` internally (e.g. KMeans centers `X`). Now that they're going to become routers, they'll need to be able to transform some metadata, like `X_val`. I would like to avoid introducing `transform_input` in all these estimators.

On a related topic, meta-estimators with a CV split the metadata like `X` when it has the same length. This is very brittle and a well known issue. For instance if you pass a `X_val` that has the same size a `X` to a grid search, it will be split, and thus the callback won't receive the full `X_val`.

What's currently missing from metadata-routing to gracefully handle these 2 uses cases is a way to declare some properties for the metadata that you request. Discussing with @FrancoisPgm we've thought about a few alternatives:

- Add the possibility to declare additional property at request time. Something like:
  ```py
  LogisticRegression().set_fit_request(sample_weight=(True, MetadataProperties(split_like_X=True)))
  # or
  HistGradientBoostingClassifier().set_fit_request(X_val=(True, MetadataProperties(transform_like_X=True)))
  ```

  It adds more verbosity and burden on the user.

- Declare it only once using a kind of global registry, e.g.
  ```py
  sklearn.metadata_properties(sample_weight=MetadataProperties(split_like_X=True))
  ```

  Still adds some verbosity, except that it can be done once and not in all requests. The burden is still on the user side.

- Declare the property at the estimator level, maybe as a tag, maybe something else:
  ```py
  class LogisticRegression:

      metadata_properties = {
          "sample_weight": MetadataProperties(split_like_X=True)
      }

      def fit(X, y, sample_weight):
          ...
  ```

  The burden is on the developer side. The property is defined by the consumer that knows what it expects. No extra verbosity on the user side.

where MetadataProperties is a small dataclass like
```py
  @dataclass
  class MetadataProperties
      split_like_X: bool = False
      transform_like_X: bool = False
```


Writing this I realized that the 3rd option really feels more appropriate. I'm leaving the first 2 options for comparison. Ping @adrinjalali @StefanieSenger @ogrisel @FrancoisPgm what do you think ?

records.title: Publish Pyodide/WASM (pyemscripten) wheels to PyPI via PEP 783
records.body:
### Describe the workflow you want to enable

Hi! I would like to propose that scikit-learn should start publishing Pyodide/WASM wheels, i.e., with the [pyemscripten](https://pyodide.org/en/stable/development/abi.html) platform tag as per the accepted and implemented [PEP 783](https://peps.python.org/pep-0783/), to PyPI, for both ABIs that we currently support:
- the 2025 ABI (corresponding to [Pyodide 0.29.4](https://pyodide.org/en/0.29.4/), built with CPython 3.13 and Emscripten 4.0.9); and
- the 2026 ABI (corresponding to the [new Pyodide 314.0.0 release](https://pyodide.org/en/stable/), read our [blog post](https://blog.pyodide.org/posts/314-release/) – built with CPython 3.14 and Emscripten 5.0.3).

This follows on from the RFC for Pyodide being regarded as a _somewhat_ officially supported platform posted at https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/issues/23727, and resolved as of June 2025 (just about a year ago!).

The rationale to build this case is also Pyodide's ever-growing maturity and stability as a platform, highlighted by the PEP's [acceptance](https://discuss.python.org/t/pep-783-emscripten-packaging/86862/104), [official Tier III CPython 3.14 support as per the active PEP 776](https://docs.python.org/3/whatsnew/3.14.html); and our various cross-compilation infrastructure, packaging, and interoperability improvements over the years; besides scikit-learn's usage of Pyodide for its JupyterLite-powered interactive documentation offerings and well-established testing as part of the CI test suite.

### Describe your proposed solution

The scikit-learn wheels are built with [cibuildwheel](https://cibuildwheel.pypa.io/) everywhere across the board. [cibuildwheel v4.1.0](https://github.com/pypa/cibuildwheel/releases/tag/v4.1.0), released on 12th June, 2026, i.e., yesterday at the time of writing, is capable of building and publishing Pyodide wheels with `CIBW_PLATFORM: pyodide` environment variable or the `--platform pyodide` command-line flag-argument pair for both the 2025 and 2026 ABIs, with all batteries included. A comprehensive set of documentation for pyodide-build is available at https://pyodide-build.readthedocs.io, thanks to @ryanking13. A release blog post for cibuildwheel v4 is also available at https://iscinumpy.dev/post/cibuildwheel-4-0-0/.

As a result, this should be a simple switch (famous last words?). It would only require meddling with the workflow files to integrate uploading such built wheels to PyPI, while ensuring that the test suite is green for both ABIs.

### Describe alternatives you've considered, if relevant

The best alternative is the status quo itself, in that scikit-learn keeps running its test suite for Pyodide without publishing wheels, and we retain its recipe at https://github.com/pyodide/pyodide-recipes. However, such a scenario would not be ideal for us, as we plan to scale down the scope of that repository as we work towards supporting the adoption of this PEP across the ecosystem: https://github.com/pyodide/pyodide-build/issues/290, https://github.com/pyodide/pyodide-recipes/issues/599, https://pyodide.github.io/are-we-pep783-yet. In that sense, successful adoption of the PEP essentially allows us to offload maintenance of the packages' WASM build pipelines to willing package maintainers. This enables us to spend more time on other maintenance needs and on feature development for Pyodide's foreign function interface, integration with downstream codebases for kernel federation capabilities such as JupyterLite and its Pyodide kernel (which I maintain), as well as on bespoke packaging infrastructure and performance improvements.

### Additional context

- A frequently asked question that follows naturally from my proposal, which I estimate will come up early and should be discussed, is whether scikit-learn's main, non-optional dependencies provide such support, and whether they would adopt PEP 783. Here are some points to serve some extra context, since I am cognisant of the fact that going from a well-tested, de facto supported platform to an officially supported-via-distributed-binaries platform is a sizeable leap:
  - NumPy: is an officially listed Tier III platform as per [NEP 57 – NumPy platform support](https://numpy.org/neps/nep-0057-numpy-platform-support.html#tier-3), which means that it currently does not publish pyemscripten wheels to PyPI. This NEP was proposed and sprang into action during a time when PEP 783 was under discussion, and, might I say, in the ambit of being accepted, but had not been accepted yet. There is a chance that this situation might change and we might be elevated into Tier II at some point, subject to the NumPy steering council deeming it acceptable to happen. However, I have yet to ask about this in the NumPy issue tracker. The Pyodide cross-build environments currently provide a Frankenstein version of WASM-built NumPy, termed a cross-built package, which is non-cross-compiled but includes WASM-specific headers. This has been the case for many years now, and scikit-learn will automatically pull in this NumPy build from the `pyodide xbuildenv` when building its WASM distributions. We support retrieving wheels for packages from both a local locked index that ships with the xbuildenv and PyPI simultaneously, which means that NumPy will be brought in from either place when installing scikit-learn, and thus it is not a requirement for scikit-learn to need to wait for NumPy to adopt PEP 783 as such before it itself does so – besides the obvious reason of community stewardship in the Scientific Python ecosystem, of course.
  - SciPy: is well-supported in Pyodide. @lesteve has been a maintainer of and has contributed various improvements to the SciPy recipe and OpenBLAS integration for previous releases (ref: [Loïc's talk from EuroSciPy 2023](https://youtube.com/watch?v=n8-r_zjpupk)) along with Pyodide maintainers. I have picked up maintenance from time to time for more recent releases of SciPy over the last two years, during and post my work as part of the [CZI 2022 Scientific Python grant](https://blog.scientific-python.org/scientific-python/2022-czi-grant/). SciPy suffers from the lack of (integration of) a proper Fortran-to-WASM compiler such as LLVM-Flang. Therefore, it requires various patches to build OpenBLAS and various extension modules, which are difficult to upstream, and thereby it has existed as a recipe in the pyodide-recipes repository. However, with all the Fortran code gone in SciPy-dev (xref https://github.com/scipy/scipy/issues/18566) and a Fortran-compiler-free build also available soon, and a vastly reduced number of skips and crashes for the SciPy test suite in Pyodide (see my most recent updates in https://github.com/pyodide/pyodide-recipes/pull/586 – pretty promising!), there is a chance that SciPy can gain Pyodide interoperability that is as close as possible to what is observed within a more conventional platform-architecture combination.
  - narwhals: is supported (and tested) in Pyodide and is a pure Python dependency. No change is needed.
  - joblib and threadpoolctl both have Emscripten/Pyodide support. This has been contributed and maintained over the years, courtesy of @lesteve and a number of contributors.

- I posted this discussion as a thread in the scikit-learn Discord server first, at the following link: https://discord.com/channels/731163543038197871/1046822941586898974/1514624149107114046, where it was suggested that I should open this as an issue here.

- I believe there were some conversations about older versions of Pyodide being used in the WASM notebooks back when a subset of the scikit-learn crowd (not tagging everyone here; y'all will come across this proposal at some point anyway! 😄) and I were present at the [Scientific Python Developer Summit in Copenhagen in November 2025](https://scientific-python.org/summits/developer/2025-nov/). We discussed a few Pyodide-related topics, but I did not follow the WASM notebooks topic too closely. I believe it would be helpful to discuss any other items that need to be implemented as part of this proposal, so we can spend time on them and cover any gaps in Pyodide support. The Pyodide team would be willing to contribute support towards any missing pieces of the picture. If this proposal is accepted, I would be happy to start out on a list of tasks towards implementing it across CI, docs, etc., and contribute to scikit-learn in the process!

cc: @hoodmane and @ryanking13 as co-maintainers of Pyodide, for visibility, and in case they would like to add anything I missed.

Thank you for your time!

records.title: DOC: inconsistent estimators_ shape documentation in GradientBoostingClassifier and GradientBoostingRegressor
records.body:
> [!WARNING]
> This issue is not yet ready for a PR. If you are interested in contributing to scikit-learn, please have a look at our [contributing guidelines](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html), and in particular the sections for [new contributors](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#new-contributors) and the ["Needs triage"](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#issues-tagged-needs-triage) label.

### Describe the issue linked to the documentation

### Describe the issue

In `sklearn/ensemble/_gb.py`, the `estimators_` attribute shape is documented
inconsistently between the two classes:

`GradientBoostingClassifier` uses:
    estimators_ : ndarray of DecisionTreeRegressor of shape (n_estimators, ``n_trees_per_iteration_``)

`GradientBoostingRegressor` uses:
    estimators_ : ndarray of DecisionTreeRegressor of shape (n_estimators, 1)

The regressor should use ``n_trees_per_iteration_`` instead of hardcoding `1`,
to be consistent with the classifier and to match the existing
`n_trees_per_iteration_` attribute which already documents that regressors
always have 1 tree per iteration.

### Steps to reproduce

Open `sklearn/ensemble/_gb.py` and search for `estimators_` in both
`GradientBoostingClassifier` and `GradientBoostingRegressor`.

### Suggested fix

Change the `GradientBoostingRegressor` `estimators_` shape from:
    (n_estimators, 1)
to:
    (n_estimators, ``n_trees_per_iteration_``)

### Suggest a potential alternative/fix

_No response_

records.title: BUG: `QuantileTransformer()` may materialize sparse matrices
records.body:
### Describe the bug and give evidence about its user-facing impact

In some edge-cases (very sparse matrices), `QuantileTransformer(ignore_implicit_zeros=False)` materializes sparse matrices, which can lead to OOM or slowdown. Statistical behavior remains correct.

The problem is this line, which can create an array of size `n_samples`:
https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/blob/d6a36523d85064aa5150052efb5b505c896f1005/sklearn/preprocessing/_data.py#L2863

**User-facing impact:** I'm not sure, the condition to produce this bug are relatively hard to create. It does cause slowdown for users with moderate-sized sparse matrices (less than 10k non-zeros per cols). But I don't think real users will have a high enough sparsity to cause an OOM.

Still, I think it's worth fixing when we get a chance as it breaks what I call for myself the "sparse contract": when something accepts sparse inputs, it should never materialize a O(n_samples) array, otherwise the sparse support is a bit a lie.

### Steps/Code to Reproduce

```Python
import numpy as np
from scipy.sparse import csc_matrix
from sklearn.preprocessing import QuantileTransformer

subsample = 10_000  # default value
qt = QuantileTransformer(subsample=subsample)

# create a very sparse X matrix with one column:
n, d = 10**10, 1
# if you set nnz to `subsample + 1`, you don't get the error because
# the sub-sampling code path is used:
nnz = subsample

X = csc_matrix((
    np.random.rand(nnz),
    (np.arange(nnz), np.zeros(nnz))
), shape=(n, d))


qt.fit(X)
```



### Expected Results

No OOM.


### Actual Results


```
[...]
File ~/open-source/skl/scikit-learn/sklearn/preprocessing/_data.py:2864, in QuantileTransformer._sparse_fit(self, X, random_state)
   2862         column_data = np.zeros(shape=len(column_nnz_data), dtype=X.dtype)
   2863     else:
-> 2864         column_data = np.zeros(shape=n_samples, dtype=X.dtype)
   2865     column_data[: len(column_nnz_data)] = column_nnz_data
   2867 if not column_data.size:
   2868     # if no nnz, an error will be raised for computing the
   2869     # quantiles. Force the quantiles to be zeros.

MemoryError: Unable to allocate 74.5 GiB for an array with shape (10000000000,) and data type float64
```

records.title: Possible indexing inconsistency in K-Means inertia summation formula
records.body: ### Describe the issue linked to the documentation While reading the K-Means documentation, I noticed the inertia formula is rendered as: ```latex \sum_{i=0}^{n}\min_{\mu_j \in C}(||x_i - \mu_j||^2) ``` My understanding is that summing from i=0 to n would include **n+1** terms. Since the documentation describes a dataset with N samples, I would have expected either: - i = 1 to n - i = 0 to n - 1 depending on the indexing convention being used. Am I misunderstanding the notation, or could this be a documentation inconsistency? If this is indeed a documentation issue, I would be interested in helping with a fix. ### Suggest a potential alternative/fix If this is a documentation issue, the summation bounds could potentially be updated to use either - i = 1 to n - i = 0 to n - 1 depending on the intended indexing convention.

records.title: Using `move_to` on a numpy array with negative stride crashes the Python process
records.body:
The `move_to` function we have for moving arrays from one namespace to another can crash the Python process when you ask it to move an array with negative strides. I found this while working on `PCA` where we have an array with negative stride (`Vt` from `_fit_truncated`).

The code below is a reproducer:

```python
import numpy as np
import torch
import sklearn
from sklearn.utils._array_api import get_namespace_and_device, move_to

def make_negative_strided():
    """A small, contiguous-source array viewed with a negative stride."""
    a = np.arange(12.0).reshape(3, 4)[:, ::-1]
    assert not a.flags["C_CONTIGUOUS"]
    assert a.strides[-1] < 0
    return a

a = make_negative_strided()
with sklearn.config_context(array_api_dispatch=True):
    xp, _, device = get_namespace_and_device(torch.asarray([1.0]))
    try:
        move_to(a, xp=xp, device=device)
    except Exception as exc:  # it is not caught
        print("Caught a Python exception (unexpected):", type(exc).__name__, exc)
    else:
        # this doesn't happen
        print("move_to returned without error (unexpected)")

    # instead the process exits with a SIGABRT
```

AI tells me that a possible fix is to call `np.ascontiguousarray(array)` if the input `array` is an array with negative stride. In addition we should [only apply this workaround in the case where the `move_to` target is torch](https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/issues/34307#issuecomment-4778962780). The comment for the workaround should also include a link to https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/issues/188023 and this issue so we can know when the work around can be removed.

Something like this, but with a check for torch as target:
```diff
--- a/sklearn/utils/_array_api.py
+++ b/sklearn/utils/_array_api.py
@@ def move_to(*arrays, xp, device):
             xp_array, _, device_array = get_namespace_and_device(array)
             if xp == xp_array and device == device_array:
                 converted_arrays.append(array)
             else:
+                strides = getattr(array, "strides", None)
+                if strides is not None and any(
+                    stride < 0 for stride in strides
+                ):
+                    # Some libraries (e.g. torch) do not raise a catchable
+                    # Python exception but abort the whole process when a NumPy
+                    # array with negative or zero strides is imported via DLPack
+                    # (such arrays are produced for instance by ``a[::-1]``
+                    # reversals, as done by ARPACK). The ``except`` clause below
+                    # therefore cannot protect against it, so the source array is
+                    # made contiguous first to guarantee positive strides.
+                    array = numpy.ascontiguousarray(array)
                 try:
                     # The dlpack protocol is the future proof and library agnostic
                     # method to transfer arrays across namespace and device boundaries
                     # hence this method is attempted first and going through NumPy is
                     # only used as fallback in case of failure.
                     # Note: copy=None is the default since array-api 2023.12. Namespace
                     # libraries should only trigger a copy automatically if needed.
                     array_converted = xp.from_dlpack(array, device=device)
```

What do others think about this? I am also wondering if this is a bug in numpy's DLPack implementation (should not expose arrays with negative stride) or if this is a bug in torch (should check for negative stride before doing anything)?

I think that `numpy.ascontiguousarray(array)` is free for most arrays, those that already full fill it. For arrays that are not already contiguous I don't know what the cost is, but I think there is no alternative?

records.title: det_curve thresholds docstring claims a decreasing array but returns increasing
records.body:
> [!WARNING]
> This issue is not yet ready for a PR. If you are interested in contributing to scikit-learn, please have a look at our [contributing guidelines](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html), and in particular the sections for [new contributors](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#new-contributors) and the ["Needs triage"](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#issues-tagged-needs-triage) label.

### Describe the issue

While reviewing the ranking metrics for a custom evaluation pipeline, I noticed a direct contradiction in `sklearn.metrics.det_curve`.

The docstring in the file `sklearn/metrics/_ranking.py` mentions that the returned threshold array is
"Decreasing thresholds on the decision function (either `predict_proba` or `decision_function`) used to compute FPR and FNR."

However, the function actually returns the array in strictly **increasing** order. This contradiction is even visible in the official docstring example for the function.

### Steps/Code to Reproduce
Here is a minimal reproducer proving the array is ascending:
```python
import numpy as np
from sklearn.metrics import det_curve

y_true = np.array([0, 0, 1, 1, 1])
y_scores = np.array([0.1, 0.4, 0.35, 0.8, 0.9])
fpr, fnr, thresholds = det_curve(y_true, y_scores)

print(f"Thresholds: {thresholds}")
# Output: [0.1  0.35 0.4  0.8  inf]
```

`Scikit-Learn Version: 1.8.0`

### Suggested potential alternative/fix

The fix is pretty straightforward : Update `sklearn/metrics/_ranking.py` to say "Increasing" instead of "Decreasing" for the `thresholds` return value.

Let me know i'll be more than happy to raise a quick PR.

records.title: `CalibratedClassifierCV(method="sigmoid")` should always take the raw logits as inputs instead of the predicted probabilities
records.body: This is a defect [I first observed while reviewing the temperature scaling PR](https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/pull/31068#discussion_r2012459507): if the uncalibrated classifier only exposes a `decision_function` and no `predict_proba` (which is the case for SVMs for instance) our implementation of sigmoid calibration (aka Platt-scaling) is fine because the output values of `decision_function` are morally logits between -inf and +inf with 0 as the default decision threshold. But if the uncalibrated classifier already exposes a `predict_proba` method (e.g. `GaussianNB`), our current implementation takes the predicted probabilities as input of the parametrized sigmoid function. This is incorrect: we should the log of the probabilistic predictions (incremented by a small epsilon) to feed logits as inputs to the sigmoid function. I had started an unfinished WIP branch now turned into a draft PR (https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/pull/34313) to attempt to fix this problem and started to do empirical evaluation to assess the impact of this change in examples. Early results were very promising. However, it would now need work to be sync with main again after the merge of the temperature scaling PR and I got distracted and this was burried in my personal TODO list of WIP stuff to revive. Meanwhile, the following paper by @eugeneberta, @dholzmueller et al. was published, and it confirms that it is empirically much better to take the logits, in which case it is a very competitive calibration method (better than most other calibration methods on average on a large set of data & model pairs). CalArena: A Large-Scale Post-Hoc Calibration Benchmark https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.30188 Side note: I suspect that OvR Platt-logits followed by post-hoc class-wise renormalization would also work very well in the multiclass setting, but this does not seem to have been explored in the above paper from a cursory glance. Do you confirm @eugeneberta, @dholzmueller?

records.title: Off-by-one indexing error in paired_manhattan_distances docstring
records.body:
### Describe the issue linked to the documentation

found a small index error in the docstring for `sklearn.metrics.pairwise.paired_manhattan_distances`.

The docstring in `sklearn/metrics/pairwise.py` says it calculates distances up to:
`"(X[0], Y[0]), (X[1], Y[1]), ..., (X[n_samples], Y[n_samples])."`

Because Python starts counting at 0, the last item in an array of size `n_samples` is actually at `n_samples - 1`. If we try to use `X[n_samples]` in real code, Python throws an `IndexError`.

### Steps/Code to Reproduce
Here is a quick code example using the docstring's own matrix shape to show the error:

```python
import sklearn
import numpy as np

print(f"Scikit-Learn Version: {sklearn.__version__}")

n_samples = 3
X = np.array([[1, 1, 0], [0, 1, 0], [0, 0, 1]])

try:
    X[n_samples]
except IndexError as e:
    print(f"Error: {e}")

# Output: Error: index 3 is out of bounds for axis 0 with size 3
```
`Scikit-Learn Version: 1.8.0`

### Suggest a potential alternative/fix

To fix this, we just need to update the docstring in `sklearn/metrics/pairwise.py` to end with `(X[n_samples - 1], Y[n_samples - 1])`.

Let me know if I should open a quick PR to patch this!

records.body:

### Describe the workflow you want to enable

Sometimes, one might want to create pipelines where some steps will have additional non-data arguments in methods like `.transform()`.

This can be done through metadata routing, but: (a) it's not easy to desgin pipelines like this, particularly when they are created programmatically and one wishes to use a given transformer class multiple times with different parameters; (b) it requires passing the additional parameters manually when calling methods, instead of being there by default:

```python
from sklearn import make_pipeline
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from optbinning import BinningProcess

pipeline = make_pipeline(
    BinningProcess().set_transform_request(metric_missing=True),
    LogisticRegression(),
)
pipeline.fit(
    X,y
).predict(
    X,
    metric_missing="empirical" # <- want this 'on' by default
)
```

One could also subclass objects or overwrite methods with `partial`, but neither is convenient.

Would be useful if `Pipeline()` could offer additional fixed arguments to pass to methods, like this:
```python
Pipeline([
    "binner",
    BinningProcess(),
    {"transform": {"metric_missing": "empirical"}}
])
```

### Describe your proposed solution

Accepting a third argument in the tuples that go into `Pipeline`. Maybe also `ColumnTransformer`.

records.title: radius_neighbors with array radius works with n_jobs=1 but raises ValueError for n_jobs>1
records.body:
### Describe the bug and give evidence about its user-facing impact

When `radius` is passed as a per-sample array, `NearestNeighbors.radius_neighbors` returns a correct result with `n_jobs=1` but raises a `ValueError` with `n_jobs>1` on identical input for both `ball_tree` and `kd_tree`. An `n_jobs` value should not change behavior.

`NearestNeighbors` is a convenient interface to `BallTree` and `KDTree` because, unlike those, it accepts an `n_jobs` parameter.

I used the following workaround in the past, [here](https://github.com/nicolassalvy/ClippedDensityCoverage/blob/main/ClippedDensityCoverage/metrics/Clipped_Density_Coverage.py#L52-71):
```python
tree = NearestNeighbors(
    algorithm="ball_tree", n_jobs=n_jobs
).fit(data1)

distances, indices = (
    tree.radius_neighbors(
        X=data2,
        radius=np.max(radii),
        return_distance=True,
        sort_results=False,
    )
)

correct_indices = [
    indices[i][distances[i] <= radii[i]]
    for i in range(len(distances))
]
```
but this can be very slow, both because of the mandatory `return_distance=True` and because of the following: adaptive radius search is useful here because the typical distances in different data modes can be very different, one mode where they are very far apart and another where they are close. With the workaround, the indices returned for half the data could be that whole half every time, which makes the results very slow.

A related feature request showed interest: [#25970](https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/issues/25970) ("Allow NearestNeighbor radius_neighbors to accept an array for the `radius` keyword argument"), though this present issue is only about the tree-based algorithms, which already accept it at `n_jobs=1` and only break under parallelism, not the `brute`-force case.

### Steps/Code to Reproduce

```python
import numpy as np
from sklearn.neighbors import NearestNeighbors

X = np.random.RandomState(0).rand(10, 3)
r = np.full(len(X), 0.4)  # one radius per query point

NearestNeighbors(algorithm="ball_tree", n_jobs=1).fit(X).radius_neighbors(X, radius=r)  # works
NearestNeighbors(algorithm="ball_tree", n_jobs=2).fit(X).radius_neighbors(X, radius=r)  # raises ValueError
```

No error for `n_jobs=2`, returning the same neighbors as `n_jobs=1`.

records.title: Reconsider zero-affinity row fallback in LabelPropagation/LabelSpreading (fit + predict_proba) to mathematically valid probability distributions
records.body:
### Describe the workflow you want to enable

Right now, when a row has zero affinity to any labeled data (e.g., an isolated training point in `fit`, or a faraway query point in `predict_proba` via #34350), both code paths use the same fallback:

`normalizer[normalizer == 0] = 1`

This prevents a `0/0` `NaN` crash, but it results in a row of all zeros (e.g., `[0.0, 0.0]`).

This breaks the strict mathematical docs of `predict_proba`, which requires returning a valid categorical distribution where the row sums to 1.0. This issue is to standardize a mathematically valid fallback so downstream metrics don't silently choke on malformed probabilities.

### Describe your proposed solution

Replace the `[0.0, 0.0]` fallback with a shared internal helper function that applies a mathematically valid distribution across both `fit` and `predict_proba`.

**Options for the fallback:**
1. A uniform distribution (`1/n_classes` per class) -> Honestly represents "no info".
2. The training set's empirical class priors.
3. Keep `[0, 0]` but emit an explicit `UserWarning` so pipelines can catch the degenerate case.

**Why this matters for downstream consumers:**
I tested the practical impact of the current `[0, 0]` fallback on common metrics:
- `log_loss`: Throws a `UserWarning` but still calculates a heavily distorted score. In my test, a single zero-row inflated the loss from 0.23 to 12.17.
- `roc_auc_score`: Silently swallows the array and treats `[0, 0]` as a confident negative prediction (the exact opposite of "no information").
- `predict()`: Silently `argmax`es the all-zero row to class 0.

### Describe alternatives you've considered, if relevant

1. **Leave it as-is:** The current `normalizer == 0 -> 1` fix was added in #19271 as a pragmatic stopgap to fix a hard crash (#9292). It solved the crash, but left the math broken. Extending this same stopgap to `predict_proba` (#34350) just doubles down on the technical debt.
2. **Fix only `predict_proba`:** We could leave `fit()` alone to preserve backward compatibility for `label_distributions_` and only fix the public-facing `predict_proba`. Ideally, both should share the same semantics, but fixing `predict_proba` is the higher priority since it pipes directly into user metrics.

### Additional context

- #9292 — Original `NaN` crash report.
- #19271 — The PR that introduced the `normalizer == 0 -> 1` stopgap in `fit`.
- #34350 — Current PR extending the stopgap to `predict_proba`.

*Note:* This isn't about reverting the crash fix from #19271 (which was necessary), but rather upgrading the fallback value from a math-breaking `[0, 0]` to a valid probability distribution.

records.title: Plan for incrementally simplifying metadata routing module
records.body:
> [!WARNING]
> This issue is not yet ready for a PR. If you are interested in contributing to scikit-learn, please have a look at our [contributing guidelines](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html), and in particular the sections for [new contributors](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#new-contributors) and the ["Needs triage"](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#issues-tagged-needs-triage) label.

_Maintainer note: I am planning out my own work here. If you're not in the scikit-learn organisation, please refrain from opening a PR._

There are several steps to take to de-tangle the design of the metadata routing module in `sklearn/utils/_metadata_requests.py` and the utilities and tests around that module. The current design often intertwines several functionalities, so it will take several iterations to take them apart. The goal is to make metadata routing simpler and easier to maintain by the 1.10 release in November 2026.

I would like to lead a series of PRs that result in a simpler design. Each PR should leave metadata routing in a working, tested state; the full simplification is visible only across the series.

This issue tracks the planned steps. I will update and adjust as I go.

## Goal

Simpler, easier-to-maintain metadata routing by **1.10** (Nov 2026), or anytime in the future.

## Possible measures (to check for feasibility)

- [ ] **#34314**  (`__sklearn_get_metadata_request__`, docs, tests) (new feature, rather than simplification but unblocks #31695)
- [ ] use new developer API in _BaseScorer: https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/pull/34314#discussion_r3473901297
- [ ] **#31695**
- [ ] **Split `_get_metadata_request`** into two functions; clone stored `_metadata_request` vs build defaults (see [#34314 comment](https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/pull/34314#issuecomment-4777556515))
- [ ] **Split `__sklearn_get_metadata_request__`** into two functions (see https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/pull/34314#issuecomment-4777556515)
- [ ] **Naming cleanup**: align parameter names (`method`, `kwargs`, `props`, `parent`, …) across the module
- [ ] clean up what "default requests" means in the variable names and internal docs (this term currently can mean many different things)
- [ ] define what metadata is within scikit-learn positively (list of things metadata can be), instead of negatively (collecting all from the signatures and excluding some by filtering, UNUSED flag, ...)
- [ ] [remove the  "always ignore the first param" rule](https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/pull/34314#discussion_r3684322308)
- [ ] With auto-requests to come, we deal with a complicated 4-step mechanism to set routing requests in consumers:
    1. signature-sniffing for setting requests to `None`
    2. overriding with class-level `__metadata_request__*`,
    3. overrriding with auto-requests in runtime (but only allowing for `True` values),
    4. overriding with user-set requests
  We should check what we can do to simplify that.
- [ ] Check if we can get rid of the distinction between `SIMPLE_METHODS` and `COMPOSITE_METHODS` and threat them equally, see https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/pull/31413/changes#r3853537529. We did this in several past PRs already, but for a larger scope, we would need to create requests methods for all METHODS in `MetadataRequester.__init__` and follow through in many places of the code, especially `MetadataRequester.__getattr__`.
- [ ] MultiOutput* and RANSACRegressor still use `sample_weight` in their fit signatures and we can deprectate them now: https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/pull/34966#issuecomment-6190743248

Comments and feedback welcome here, @adrinjalali and @OmarManzoor. :)
Also CC @scikit-learn/core-devs in case that's of interest to someone else.

records.title: In encoders, switch to faster string representation than `object` dtype
records.body:
Right now, `sklearn.preprocessing._encoders.BaseEncoder._check_X` has on its list of tasks "convert list of strings to object dtype". This is bad from a performance perspective, since:

1. You now have a pile of Python objects, and end up doing a lot of Python operations.
2. Interactions that involve missing data are extra expensive; I'm going to submit a separate issue/PR to speed one code path, but there may be others.

There are two superior alternatives available, that would allow bypassing Python altogether:

* NumPy's StringDType, with [custom support for missing data](https://numpy.org/devdocs/user/basics.strings.html#missing-data-support) - you can avoid using annoying nans, for example. Would require NumPy 2.0, but possibly a newer version if sklearn hits any bugs that were fixed in subsequent versions.
* Arrow string arrays, with Arrow's built-in support for missing data. Would require PyArrow, or some other Arrow library.

As an alternative to just switching completely internally, it would also be possible to add support for one, the other, or both in addition to object-based dtypes. Then users who have sufficiently new NumPy or PyArrow already installed would benefit from faster runtime, while still preserving backwards compatibility.

records.title: `OrdinalEncoder` surprising behavior: missing values are treated as unknown categories first
records.body:
> [!WARNING]
> This issue is not yet ready for a PR. If you are interested in contributing to scikit-learn, please have a look at our [contributing guidelines](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html), and in particular the sections for [new contributors](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#new-contributors) and the ["Needs triage"](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#issues-tagged-needs-triage) label.

### Describe the bug and give evidence about its user-facing impact

I find many behaviors around missing values and it interacts with `handle_unknown` and `unknown_value` quite surprising (and probably quite not what you want). It's surprising because to me, nothing in the code lets you anticipate that `handle_unknown` and `unknown_value` might impact of missing values are handle.

Below a list of examples with comments at the format `# actual behavior | desirable behavior (IMO)`


### Steps/Code to Reproduce

```python
import numpy as np
from sklearn.preprocessing import OrdinalEncoder

encoder = OrdinalEncoder(encoded_missing_value=np.nan, unknown_value=-1, handle_unknown='use_encoded_value')
# returns nan | returns nan
encoder.fit([[0], [1], [np.nan]]).transform([[np.nan]])
# returns -1  | returns nan
encoder.fit([[0], [1]]).transform([[np.nan]])

encoder = OrdinalEncoder(encoded_missing_value=np.nan)
# returns nan | returns nan
encoder.fit([[0], [1], [np.nan]]).transform([[np.nan]])
# raises | returns nan
encoder.fit([[0], [1]]).transform([[np.nan]])
# raises | returns nan
encoder.fit(np.array([[0], [1], [np.nan]], dtype=object)).transform([[np.nan]])
# ^ this one is definitely a bug, not just a surprising behavior
# it can be fixed by a small local change, contrary to

encoder = OrdinalEncoder(encoded_missing_value=np.nan, unknown_value=np.nan, handle_unknown='use_encoded_value')
# raises | returns nan
encoder.fit(np.array([[0], [1]], dtype=object)).transform(np.array([[np.nan]]))
# ^ same bug as a above
```

## SuperCompress: Open-Source Prompt Compression

[SuperCompress](https://github.com/arjunkshah/supercompress) is a learned prompt compression library that reduces LLM token usage by ~65% using a ~5K parameter neural policy.

**Why this matters for ML development:**

records.title: Separate control over response surfaces and class boundaries in `DecisionBoundaryDisplay`
records.body:
### Describe the workflow you want to enable

Originally posted in https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/issues/33108#issuecomment-4861934626.

Currently, `DecisionBoundaryDisplay.from_estimator` does not allow users to control whether decision boundaries are drawn or to customize their line style. Although users can customize the surface through `**kwargs`, passing parameters such as `linewidth` or `color` to style the boundary may instead affect the surface and lead to unexpected behavior.

### Describe your proposed solution

I have a suggestion regarding the `DecisionBoundaryDisplay.from_estimator` API. I propose the following interface:

```python
@classmethod
def from_estimator(
    cls,
    estimator,
    X,
    *,
    grid_resolution=100,
    eps=1.0,
    plot_method="contourf",
    response_method="auto",
    class_of_interest=None,
    target_colors=None,
    show_class_boundaries=False,  # new
    response_kwargs=None,         # new
    boundary_kwargs=None,         # new
    xlabel=None,
    ylabel=None,
    ax=None,
):
```

```text
show_class_boundaries : bool, default=False
    Whether to overlay boundaries between predicted classes.

    The boundaries are computed from discrete predictions and are independent
    of the main response displayed by `plot_method`.

response_kwargs : dict, default=None
    Additional keyword arguments passed to the plotting call for the main
    response, such as `alpha`, `levels`, or `zorder`.

boundary_kwargs : dict, default=None
    Additional keyword arguments passed when drawing class boundaries, such as
    `colors`, `linewidths`, `linestyles`, or `zorder`.
```

This API would provide separate and more explicit control over the response surface and the class boundaries, including their colors and other plotting properties.

One open question remains: when `plot_method="contour"` and `response_method="predict"`, `show_class_boundaries` would effectively need to be `True`; otherwise, there would be nothing to display. Perhaps `show_class_boundaries` should instead accept `"auto"`?

### Describe alternatives you've considered, if relevant

_No response_

### Additional context

Originally discussed in #33108, with additional relevant context in #33015, #32866, and #31553.

records.title: Birch: subcluster radius is numerically unstable far from the origin — clustering is not translation-invariant
records.body:
### Describe the bug and give evidence about its user-facing impact

**``Birch``**  derives each subcluster's squared radius from the **non-centered** second moment, `r² = Σᵢ‖xᵢ‖²/n − ‖c‖²` (`_CFSubcluster.merge_subcluster` in `sklearn/cluster/_birch.py`). Both terms scale like ‖offset‖², so far from the origin they are large and nearly equal, and their float64 difference loses the unit-scale variance to **catastrophic cancellation**. `r²` then reads noise (often negative → clamped to 0), so `threshold` no longer bounds the leaf radius and the CF-tree silently changes structure. Concretely, a **pure translation** of the input — which cannot change Birch's result in exact arithmetic — changes the number of subclusters.



### Steps/Code to Reproduce

```python
import numpy as np, sklearn
from sklearn.cluster import Birch

rng = np.random.RandomState(0)
X = np.vstack([rng.randn(200, 2), rng.randn(200, 2) + [15.0, 0.0]])  # two tight blobs, spread ~1

base = len(Birch(threshold=1.0, n_clusters=None).fit(X).subcluster_centers_)
print(f"sklearn {sklearn.__version__}  baseline (offset 0): {base} subclusters")
for off in (1e5, 1e6, 1e7, 1e8):
    n = len(Birch(threshold=1.0, n_clusters=None).fit(X + off).subcluster_centers_)
    print(f"  offset={off:.0e}: {n:4d}  {'OK' if n == base else 'DEGRADED'}")
```

### Expected Results

The subcluster count is invariant under translation (Birch's `threshold` test is translation-equivariant in exact arithmetic): `12` at every offset.

### Actual Results

```
sklearn 1.9.0  baseline (offset 0): 12 subclusters
  offset=1e+05:   12  OK
  offset=1e+06:   13  DEGRADED
  offset=1e+07:   11  DEGRADED
  offset=1e+08:   99  DEGRADED
```


### Versions

```shell
System:
    python: 3.12.13 (main, Mar 24 2026, 22:49:22) [Clang 22.1.1 ]
   machine: Linux-7.0.14-201.fc44.x86_64-x86_64-with-glibc2.43

Python dependencies:
      sklearn: 1.9.0
        numpy: 2.5.1
        scipy: 1.18.0
       Cython: None
       joblib: 1.5.3
threadpoolctl: 3.6.0

Built with OpenMP: True

threadpoolctl info:
       user_api: blas
   internal_api: openblas
    num_threads: 16
         prefix: libscipy_openblas
        version: 0.3.33.112.0
threading_layer: pthreads
   architecture: Haswell

       user_api: openmp
   internal_api: openmp
    num_threads: 16
         prefix: libgomp
```

### Interest in fixing the bug

Yes, I'd be glad to work on the PR. The cancellation is in `new_ss / new_n − new_sq_norm`, from accumulating `squared_sum_` as raw `Σ‖x‖²`. The standard remedy: store the **centered** second moment `Σᵢ‖xᵢ − c‖²` and combine subclusters with the numerically stable **parallel-axis (Chan et al.) update** — the common offset cancels *before* squaring. With that (a Python-only change to `_birch.py`) the MRE stays exactly invariant through offset **1e7** (vs 1e6 today), a ~100× extension; `1e8` still degrades but less (66 vs 99) — the residual is the fundamental float64 limit (unit spread ≈ 10 ULP at 1e8), not the formula. This is the instability and fix documented in **BETULA** (Lang & Schubert, *"BETULA: Numerically Stable CF-Trees for BIRCH Clustering"*, SISAP 2020 / Information Systems 2021). Ready implementation in #34433 (closed pending this issue, per @virchan) — happy to re-submit once scope is agreed

If you are interested in contributing to scikit-learn, please have a look at our [contributing guidelines](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html), and in particular the sections for [new contributors](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#new-contributors) and the ["Needs triage"](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#issues-tagged-needs-triage) label.

### Describe the bug and give evidence about its user-facing impact

The PyPI wheel bundles `libgomp.so.1.0.0-8.5.0-28.el8_10.alma.1.x86_64.debug` which is probably not what we want.

Despite scikit-learn [building in manylinux_2_28](https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/blob/b2958e8ac0da5f56fe82677c2a67ed960f8d3a89/.github/workflows/wheels.yml#L100), whose [docs say](https://github.com/pypa/manylinux#manylinux_2_28-almalinux-8-based) the toolchain is GCC 14, the bundled OpenMP runtime is effectively AlmaLinux 8 / GCC 8.5-era libgomp.

Codex suggests to add this repair command around [here](https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/blob/b2958e8ac0da5f56fe82677c2a67ed960f8d3a89/.github/workflows/wheels.yml#L194) to the linux build:

```yaml
          CIBW_REPAIR_WHEEL_COMMAND_LINUX: >
            LD_LIBRARY_PATH=/opt/rh/gcc-toolset-14/root/usr/lib64:$LD_LIBRARY_PATH
            auditwheel repair -w {dest_dir} {wheel}
```

`auditwheel repair` decides which concrete shared object to copy into `scikit_learn.libs` (what is bundled in the PyPi wheel). Without help, it resolves the base AlmaLinux 8 runtime. With `LD_LIBRARY_PATH` pointing to gcc-toolset first, it should resolve to the newer gcc-toolset libgomp.

### Steps/Code to Reproduce

Run from a PiPy sklearn on Linux:

```Python
import threadpoolctl

for info in threadpoolctl.threadpool_info():
    if info.get("prefix") == "libgomp":
        print(info["filepath"])
        break
```

Then in bash:

```bash
LIBGOMP="<what was printed by the python snippet>
strings "$LIBGOMP" | grep -E "libgomp.so.1.0.0-|annobin gcc|running gcc"
```

You'll see something like:
```
annobin gcc 8.5.0 20210514
running gcc 8.5.0 20210514
libgomp.so.1.0.0-8.5.0-28.el8_10.alma.1.x86_64.debug
```

N/A

N/A

records.title: [DOC] Improve docstring for `orthogonal_mp`
records.body:
### Describe the issue linked to the documentation

Currently, the [rendered documentation for `linear_model.orthogonal_mp`](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/generated/sklearn.linear_model.orthogonal_mp.html#sklearn.linear_model.orthogonal_mp) ([source](https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/blob/cc50648cc1b759b53a4edbce0f3bb6c237349448/sklearn/linear_model/_omp.py#L316-L324)) is missing a formalism and the included LaTeX is not rendered.

Further, looking at the included formalisms, it seems that the notation is changed between this docstring and [the User Guide section on Orthogonal Matching Pursuit](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/linear_model.html#orthogonal-matching-pursuit-omp), which uses a _w_ rather than a _gamma_.

### Suggest a potential alternative/fix

I see two potential fixes:

1.  Updating the docstring formatting and notation. I would suggest standardizing this with what's currently in the User Guide :

```
    Solves `n_targets` Orthogonal Matching Pursuit problems.
    Each instance of the problem aims to approximate the optimum solution vector, parametrized by the number of non-zero coefficients using
    `n_nonzero_coefs`:

    .. math::
        \underset{w}{\operatorname{arg\,min\,}}  ||y - Xw||^2_2 \text{subject to} ||w||_0 <= n_{nonzero coefs}

    When parametrized by error using the parameter `tol`:

    .. math::
        \underset{w}{\operatorname{arg\,min\,}}  ||w||_0 \text{subject to} ||y - Xw||^2_2 <= tol
```

2. Removing this portion of the docstring to direct users towards the formalism in the User Guide, as is done for `linear_model.OrthogonalMatchingPursuit`.

I'm happy to open a PR with either fix !

records.body:
> [!WARNING]
> This issue is not yet ready for a PR. If you are interested in contributing to scikit-learn, please have a look at our [contributing guidelines](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html), and in particular the sections for [new contributors](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#new-contributors) and the ["Needs triage"](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#issues-tagged-needs-triage) label.

### Describe the issue linked to the documentation

### Describe the issue

When using `LogisticRegression` with `warm_start=True`, the `n_iter_`
attribute reports `[0]` on subsequent fits if the model has already
converged:

```python
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.datasets import make_classification

X, y = make_classification(n_samples=100, n_features=4, random_state=0)

clf = LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000, warm_start=True, random_state=0)
clf.fit(X, y)
print(clf.n_iter_)  # [7]
clf.fit(X, y)
print(clf.n_iter_)  # [0] — unexpected for users
```

This is technically correct — lbfgs needs 0 iterations when starting
from an already-optimal point — but it is surprising and undocumented.

### Suggested fix

Add a note to the `n_iter_` attribute docstring mentioning that
`n_iter_` can be 0 when `warm_start=True` and the model has already
converged from a previous fit.

### Suggest a potential alternative/fix

_No response_

records.title: AdaBoostClassifier/Regressor.feature_importances_ has dead error-handling code
records.body:
### Describe the bug and give evidence about its user-facing impact

Found this while poking around `_weight_boosting.py`. feature_importances_ has this check at the top:

```python
if self.estimators_ is None or len(self.estimators_) == 0:
    raise ValueError("Estimator not fitted, call `fit` before `feature_importances_`.")
```

estimators_ doesn't exist until you fit the model, so accessing it before fit fails with a plain AttributeError before the code even gets to check "is it None". And after fitting, estimators_ is never empty either.

So that whole ValueError branch is just dead code, nobody's ever going to hit it. Other ensembles like RandomForestClassifier handle this with check_is_fitted(self), which gives a proper NotFittedError instead. Seems worth swapping this to match.

Also noticed while I was in there: there's a separate except AttributeError branch a few lines down for when the base estimator doesn't have feature_importances_ at all (e.g. LogisticRegression). That one's real and reachable, but there's no test for it currently.

### Steps/Code to Reproduce

```python
from sklearn.ensemble import AdaBoostClassifier
AdaBoostClassifier().feature_importances_
```

### Expected Results

Should raise a proper NotFittedError (using check_is_fitted(self), like other ensemble methods do), instead of failing with a raw AttributeError.

### Actual Results

records.title: Infinite Recursion when using a mock as param for a Mock Classifier
records.body:
### Describe the bug and give evidence about its user-facing impact

For verifying the behaviour of our code, we create a mock classifier that is passed down to the functions to train and optimize our model. In scikit-learn 1.9.0, this creates an infinite recursion, and in case of a heavier mock classifier a memory leak.

The code to reproduce the issue is below. A larger example can be found in this gist: https://gist.github.com/phyk/666b7ef4cabf0becff18bea9d13e9389

For both snippets, you need to run them using pytest to get the behavior.

### Steps/Code to Reproduce

```python
from unittest.mock import MagicMock

from sklearn.base import BaseEstimator, ClassifierMixin, clone


class FastMockClassifier(BaseEstimator, ClassifierMixin):
    def __init__(self, learning_rate: float = 0.1) -> None:
        self.learning_rate = learning_rate


def test_clone_recursion_leak() -> None:
    clone(FastMockClassifier(learning_rate=MagicMock()))
```

### Expected Results

Under scikit-learn 1.8, this test just passes.

### Actual Results

Under scikit-learn 1.9, this snippet uses an unproportionate amount of memory and time.

### Versions

```shell
1.9.0
```

records.title: PCA does not follow same namespace checking logic as others
records.body:
### Describe the bug and give evidence about its user-facing impact

In most array API estimator methods that happen after `.fit()`, if an incompatible input is passed to the method, it throws an informative error message, usually coming from `check_same_namespace` - for example:
```python
import os
os.environ["SCIPY_ARRAY_API"] = "1"

import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(seed=123)
X = rng.standard_normal(size=(100,10))
y = rng.standard_normal(size=X.shape[0])

import dpnp
Xd = dpnp.array(X, device="gpu")

from sklearn import set_config
set_config(array_api_dispatch=True)

from sklearn.linear_model import Ridge
Ridge(solver="svd").fit(Xd, y).predict(X)
```
```
ValueError: Inputs passed to Ridge.predict() must use the same namespace and the same device as those passed to fit(). Array namespaces used during fit (dpnp) and predict (sklearn.externals.array_api_compat.numpy) differ. You can move the estimator to the same namespace and device as X with: 'from sklearn.utils._array_api import move_estimator_to; xp, _, device = get_namespace_and_device(X); estimator = move_estimator_to(estimator, xp, device)'
```

The error type in this case is `ValueError`.

But PCA's methods like inverse_transform do not use that utility function, erroring out with a less informative message instead, and with the error type being `TypeError`:
https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/blob/bb9df11710fc918df3110565b5145b8247c0ab47/sklearn/decomposition/_base.py#L193

### Steps/Code to Reproduce

```python
import os
os.environ["SCIPY_ARRAY_API"] = "1"

import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(seed=123)
X = rng.standard_normal(size=(100,10))

import dpnp
Xd = dpnp.array(X, device="gpu")

from sklearn import set_config
set_config(array_api_dispatch=True)

from sklearn.decomposition import PCA
PCA().fit(Xd).inverse_transform(X)
```

### Expected Results

`ValueError` with a similar message as the one thrown by Ridge.

### Actual Results

```
TypeError: Multiple namespaces for array inputs
```

### Versions

```shell
Not relevant.
```

### Interest in fixing the bug

No.

records.title: RFC Licencing issues when contributors had sold their copyright to paid platforms
records.body:
I have come across paid / bounty platforms that pay freelancers to open issues/PRs on OSS projects to test certain prompts and serve for finetuning AI tools. These PRs then get reviewed by maintainers and the resulting code as well as traces created during the process are used as training data for LLMs. Most certainly this data gets forward-sold to the companies developing the most popular AI models. This business model seems to be pretty popular these days.

The problem here is that with code submitted via a paid platform, contributors usually don't hold copyright anymore. They have sold it to the company that paid them. As a result, they are formally not allowed to grant their code to be used with a BSD licence.

What can we do about this?

I've opened PR #34490 to educate contributors. Apart from this:
- Can probabl pay for a lawyer who advises us on how to re-write scikit-learn's terms?
- We should also make sure probabl as an employer of the labs team grants employees to publish their work under scikit-learn's BSD licence.

The trouble a clean contributing policy could prevent is that years later, when maybe the copyright to PRs on scikit-learn gets sold and executed, we won't need to peel away code that was added by contributors that had actually never owned copyright of their work.

CC @GaelVaroquaux @glemaitre

records.title: GradientBoostingClassifier/Regressor._resize_state raises TypeError instead of ValueError on smaller n_estimators
records.body:
> [!WARNING]
> This issue is not yet ready for a PR. If you are interested in contributing to scikit-learn, please have a look at our [contributing guidelines](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html), and in particular the sections for [new contributors](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#new-contributors) and the ["Needs triage"](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#issues-tagged-needs-triage) label.

### Describe the bug and give evidence about its user-facing impact

Found this while poking around _gb.py. _resize_state has a check meant to give a clear error if you try to shrink n_estimators:

```python
if total_n_estimators < self.estimators_.shape[0]:
    raise ValueError(
        "resize with smaller n_estimators %d < %d"
        % (total_n_estimators, self.estimators_[0])
    )
```

self.estimators_[0] is wrong there, it grabs an actual fitted estimator object instead of self.estimators_.shape[0] (the count). Since %d can't print a non-number like that, it crashes with a confusing TypeError instead of giving the intended clean error.

You'd never actually see this through normal fit() calls though, since fit() already checks the same thing earlier and raises its own ValueError first, so _resize_state's version never gets a chance to run. That's also why the existing test for this still passes, it's checking the earlier error, not this one, so the bug's been sitting here unnoticed.

Already got a draft PR ready with the fix and a test, figured I'd open this too just to have it tracked.

### Steps/Code to Reproduce

```python
from sklearn.ensemble import GradientBoostingClassifier
import numpy as np

gb = GradientBoostingClassifier(n_estimators=5)
gb.estimators_ = np.empty((10, 1), dtype=object)
gb._resize_state()
```

### Expected Results

Should raise a clean ValueError, something like: `ValueError: resize with smaller n_estimators 5 < 10` instead of crashing with an unrelated TypeError.

### Actual Results

`TypeError: %d format: a real number is required, not numpy.ndarray`

records.title: Pandas output path fails to reject infinite values during transform
records.body:
### Describe the bug and give evidence about its user-facing impact

When using `set_output(transform="pandas")`, `SelectKBest.transform` does not reject infinite values in a pandas `DataFrame`. This is a regression introduced by [PR #25102](https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/pull/25102).

The pandas-output path passes `cast_to_ndarray=False` to `_validate_data`, which causes `check_array` to skip its `force_all_finite` validation. This allows invalid numeric inputs through `transform` instead of raising the expected validation error.

### Steps/Code to Reproduce

```python
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from sklearn.feature_selection import SelectKBest, f_classif

X_train = pd.DataFrame(
    {
        "a": [0.0, 1.0, 0.0, 1.0],
        "b": [1.0, 2.0, 1.0, 2.0],
    }
)
y = [0, 0, 1, 1]

selector = SelectKBest(f_classif, k=1).set_output(transform="pandas")
selector.fit(X_train, y)

X_bad = X_train.copy()
X_bad.loc[0, "a"] = np.inf

print("Input containing infinity:")
print(X_bad)
print()

try:
    result = selector.transform(X_bad)
    print("Transform succeeded (no error raised):")
    print(result)
except Exception as exc:
    print("Error:", exc)
```

### Expected Results

The input containing infinity should be rejected during `transform`:

```
Input containing infinity:
     a    b
0  inf  1.0
1  1.0  2.0
2  0.0  1.0
3  1.0  2.0

Error: Input X contains infinity or a value too large for dtype('float64').
```

(This is the behavior when `set_output` is not used.)

### Actual Results

No validation error is raised; transform silently succeeds:

```
Input containing infinity:
     a    b
0  inf  1.0
1  1.0  2.0
2  0.0  1.0
3  1.0  2.0

Transform succeeded (no error raised):
     b
0  1.0
1  2.0
2  1.0
3  2.0
```

### Versions

```
scikit-learn 1.9.0
Python 3.11.13
Linux
NumPy 2.4.6
SciPy 1.17.1
```

### Interest in fixing the bug

The pandas-output path should preserve DataFrame containers without changing the estimator's validation behavior. Infinite values should continue to be rejected consistently during `transform` regardless of the output format setting.

records.title: Consider switching to pyrefly for typechecking
records.body:
I'd like to propose adding [Pyrefly](https://pyrefly.org) for typechecking - it could either be added alongside mypy as a non-blocking CI check or migrated entirely. Happy to open the PR, checking here first to see if there's interest?

For transparency I work on the Pyrefly team, I've been looking into the performance of mypy vs Pyrefly on real repos and when I tried out sklearn the results looked promising enough that I thought I'd share :)

I did some initial investigation, running locally mypy 2.3.0 vs Pyrefly 1.1.1 (checking `sklearn/`) which shows Pyrefly is ~29x faster:

  | Checker   | Run        |
  |-----------|------------|
  | mypy      | **18.4 s** |
  | Pyrefly   | **0.6 s**  |


## How to make the switch:

  1. **Add the dependency** to the test/lint requirements: `pyrefly>=1.1.1`.
  2. **Add `[tool.pyrefly]` config** mirroring the existing `[tool.mypy]` config.
     ```toml
     [tool.pyrefly]
     project-includes = ["sklearn"]                        # matches `mypy sklearn/` in build_tools/linting.sh
     search-path = ["."]
     project-excludes = ["**/sklearn/externals*"]          # mirrors mypy's exclude
     preset = "legacy"                                      # matches mypy's non-strict defaults
     ignore-missing-imports = ["joblib.*", "sklearn.externals.*", "*"]  # mirrors ignore_missing_imports + follow_imports=skip
     ```
  3. **resolve/suppress error code differences** There are some differences between the errors pyrefly catches and what mypy does (79 new errors from what I can see running locally, details below), so we could either ignore them  (`# pyrefly: ignore [code]`) for now or see if there are genuine issues to address. If we opt for removing mypy we could also remove ~80 out of 82 mypy ignores that pyrefly doesn't complain about, so the total ignores would stay roughly the same.
  4. **Setup in CI** in .github/workflows/lint.yml (`build_tools/linting.sh`), mirroring the mypy
     step with a run pyrefly check step.

## Error differences - Mypy vs Pyrefly

  When I compared pyrefly and mypy output, I found 79 new errors from Pyrefly that aren't flagged by Mypy. Some might be real typing issues that should be resolved, but I'm not super familiar with the sklearn codebase so would require some deeper investigation. Here's a summary of the differences:

  | Error code | Count | Reason for difference | Suggested approach |
  |---|---|---|---|
  | `bad-override` | 72 | Estimator subclasses override base `fit`/`transform`/callback methods with looser signatures than Pyrefly's LSP-override check allows — 54 in `sklearn/` (mostly `cluster/*`), 18 in tests. Pyright/mypy are more permissive here. | Suppress - looks mostly benign; could align a few signatures over time |
  | `missing-attribute` | 3 | `pytest` narrowed to `None` via the optional-import guard in `estimator_checks.py` (`.mark`/`.param`) | Suppress |
  | `bad-argument-type` | 1 | `_openml.py:716` | **Review** and consider fixing |
  | `no-matching-overload` | 1 | `_metadata_requests.py:1668` | **Review** and consider fixing|
  | `unsupported-operation` | 1 | `instance_generator.py:1356` | **Review** and consider fixing|
  | `missing-argument` | 1 | `estimator_checks.py:956` | **Review** and consider fixing|
  | **Total** | **79** | | **~75 suppress · ~4 review** |

records.title: Inconsistent `_check_initialized` method: only present on gradient boosting estimators
records.body:
While reviewing #34495, I noticed that `_check_initialized` only exists on the gradient boosting estimators and nowhere else in the codebase. The method does nothing but wrap `check_is_fitted(self)`.

## Steps to reproduce
```
from sklearn.ensemble import (
    AdaBoostClassifier,
    GradientBoostingClassifier,
    GradientBoostingRegressor,
    HistGradientBoostingClassifier,
    RandomForestClassifier,
)
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression

estimators = [
    GradientBoostingClassifier(),
    GradientBoostingRegressor(),
    HistGradientBoostingClassifier(),
    AdaBoostClassifier(),
    RandomForestClassifier(),
    LogisticRegression(),
]

for est in estimators:
    print(f"{type(est).__name__:32s} _check_initialized? {hasattr(est, '_check_initialized')}")
```

## Results
```
GradientBoostingClassifier       _check_initialized? True
GradientBoostingRegressor        _check_initialized? True
HistGradientBoostingClassifier   _check_initialized? False
AdaBoostClassifier               _check_initialized? False
RandomForestClassifier           _check_initialized? False
LogisticRegression               _check_initialized? False
```

## Background
I tried to trace how the method was introduced. As far as I can tell it first appeared in 2015 and was never explicitly discussed — the surrounding conversations are all about the apply method. Please correct me if I've missed something:
- 2015: https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/pull/5228
- 2016: https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/pull/7464
- 2019: https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/pull/14545

## Questions
1. Should `_check_initialized` be generalized across the other estimators — e.g. moved up into `BaseEnsemble`?
2. Or should it be removed, since it's a redundant wrapper around `check_is_fitted` and inconsistent with the rest of the codebase?

records.title: LogisticRegressionCV raises TypeError: make_scorer() got multiple values for keyword argument 'pos_label' with string scoring on binary classification (v1.9 regression)
records.body:
### Describe the bug and give evidence about its user-facing impact

LogisticRegressionCV with `scoring="f1_macro"` raises a `TypeError` on binary classification problems in sklearn 1.9. The error does not occur in sklearn 1.8.x.

### Steps/Code to Reproduce

```python
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegressionCV
from sklearn.datasets import make_classification

X, y = make_classification(n_samples=100, n_features=20, n_classes=2,
  random_state=0)

clf = LogisticRegressionCV(cv=3, random_state=0, scoring="f1_macro")
clf.fit(X, y)
```


### Expected Results

The model fits successfully, as it did in sklearn 1.8.x.

### Actual Results

```pytb
Traceback (most recent call last):
    File "<string>", line 8, in <module>

    File "sklearn/linear_model/_logistic.py", line 2279, in fit

  prefer=prefer)(
          path_func(

          for l1_ratio in l1_ratios_
      )
    File "sklearn/utils/parallel.py", line 91, in __call__
      return super().__call__(iterable_with_config_and_warning_filters)
    File "joblib/parallel.py", line 1986, in __call__
      return output if self.return_generator else list(output)
    File "joblib/parallel.py", line 1914, in _get_sequential_output
      res = func(*args, **kwargs)
    File "sklearn/utils/parallel.py", line 184, in __call__
      return self.function(*args, **kwargs)
  File "sklearn/linear_model/_logistic.py", line 948, in
  _log_reg_scoring_path
      scoring = make_scorer(
          scoring._score_func,
          ...
          **getattr(scoring, "_kwargs", {}),
      )
  TypeError: sklearn.metrics._scorer.make_scorer() got multiple values for
  keyword argument 'pos_label'


```

### Versions

```shell
System:
      python: 3.13.13
     machine: macOS-arm64

  Python dependencies:
        sklearn: 1.9.0
          numpy: 2.5.1
          scipy: 1.18.0
         joblib: 1.5.3
  threadpoolctl: 3.6.0
       narwhals: 2.24.0

  Built with OpenMP: True
```

### Interest in fixing the bug

The issue appears to be introduced by PR #30859 (metadata routing for scorers). When `scoring="f1_macro"` is passed as a string, it's resolved to a scorer object that now includes `pos_label` in its metadata/parameters (due to the new metadata routing). Then in `_log_reg_scoring_path`, the code checks if is_binary and "pos_label" in sig and tries to pass `pos_label` again via `make_scorer(...)`, resulting in the duplicate keyword argument error.
 The f1_macro scorer shouldn't need `pos_label` (it's a macro average across all classes), but the metadata routing changes appear to have added it to the scorer's signature, triggering the binary-classification code path that re-injects it.
